#6808. The “Facial in a Bottle” Products Experts Say Actually Work

Every item on this page was chosen by an ELLE editor. We may earn commission on some of the items you choose to buy.

Your trick to recreating a salon glow at home.

First came “botox in a bottle.” Now, “facial in a bottle” is the latest catchy phrase permeating beauty aisles. Also sometimes labeled with the term “flash facial,” these “multi-functional formulas are designed to mimic the actual steps of a professional facial—think exfoliation, hydration, and brightening—all in one,” explains dermatologist Dr. Jessie Cheung. “The best ones do this by combining acids, enzymes, antioxidants, and hydrators to address multiple skin concerns while minimizing irritation.”

And while they’re not a replacement for in-office treatments and an esthetician’s skilled hand, they can “deliver instant or dramatic results, typically imparting a glow or resurfacing effect,” says New York-based facialist Samantha Susca. She adds that these multipurpose formulas can nicely complement salon visits and help extend results between appointments.

Ahead, we tapped our experts and fellow dermatologist Dr. Pearl Ugwu-Dike for their top “facial in a bottle” recommendations, and included a few picks our beauty editors use religiously. Read on for the products they say truly live up to the hype, including ones Susca uses with her own clients. Plus, expert tips for choosing the right formula for your skin type.

The path to glassier skin often starts with a good cleanser. Susca loves this option for “a gentle daily resurfacing,” noting that it helps clear congestion and remove dead skin while also hydrating, de-puffing, and reducing the look of hyperpigmentation. “Two enzymes gently exfoliate to dissolve both oil and surface keratin, while the sugar-bound vitamin C molecule (ascorbyl glucoside) is one of the most intelligent deliveries of vitamin C that brightens the skin,” she explains. “It develops into a glow-inducing, active vitamin C once the cleanser is rinsed off.” Meanwhile, ectoin, niacinamide, and caffeine help soothe the skin and reduce inflammation.

According to the brand, the water-activated, powder-to-liquid formula is best used once daily. Those with sensitive skin should start by using it for 30 seconds every other day and watch how their skin reacts before potentially increasing the frequency.

Key ingredients: Alpha hydroxy acid complex, vitamin C complex, niacinamide, ectoin, caffeine

Over-the-counter chemical peels can offer some of the powerful skin-evening effects of a professional peel. And because they’re less intense, they can be a great option for those seeking a milder treatment. “The best at-home formulas balance exfoliation with barrier support, keeping your skin brighter, smoother, and more even without irritation,” Dr. Cheung advises. She especially likes this option from Kiehl’s, which she says “combines salicylic acid, glycolic acid, and lactic acid with soothing copper gluconate for a treatment that can be used daily.”

Key Ingredients: salicylic acid, glycolic acid, lactic acid, copper gluconate

A favorite among dermatologists, estheticians, A-listers, and beauty editors, Biologique Recherche’s Lotion P50 is iconic for good reason. “This multi-acid product exfoliates while improving skin function, for immediate glow and long-term improvements,” says Dr. Cheung. The milky toner combines AHAs, BHAs, and vinegar with gluconolactone, a gentler exfoliant, and niacinamide. Together, these ingredients help remove dead skin cells, support cell turnover, regulate sebum production, and balance the skin’s pH. As the most active of the five formulas in the P50 line, it’s best suited for those with thicker or keratinized skin who can handle a stronger exfoliant. Those with thinner or more sensitive skin may prefer P50W, formulated for sensitive, oily skin, or the newer P50T.

In her review of Lotion P50 PIGM 400, formulated to target acne scars and dark marks, contributing fashion and luxury editor Moriah Polk wrote: “About a month into using P50 consistently, I walked into work, and a fellow editor stopped me mid-sentence to say my skin was glowing. And no, I wasn’t wearing makeup. What this product does best is deliver that elusive, youthful luminosity that doesn’t always photograph well but looks incredible IRL. My skin just looks fresher, brighter, and more awake—no small feat in winter, when it’s usually flaky, dull, and generally uncooperative. P50 PIGM 400 is the only thing I’ve changed in my routine, and since starting it, I haven’t had a single breakout.”

Key ingredients: gluconolactone, tartaric acid, citric acid, lactic acid, malic acid, salicylic acid, acetic acid, niacinamide

“This waxless, weightless balm-to-oil has quickly become a desert island product of mine, and a standard finishing touch in my treatments,” says Susca. “The 86 antioxidants leave the most incredible glow that mimics a 90-minute facial.” Using a blend of fruit extracts, seed oils, and emollient-rich murumuru butter, it works to protect and deeply nourish the skin while keeping it calm and balanced.

Bonus: You can also use this to prime the skin for a gua sha session.

Key ingredients: Murumuru butter, elderberry fruit extract, blueberry seed oil, green tea leaf extract

“At just $30, these peeling pads take a remarkably comprehensive approach,” says Dr. Ugwu-Dike. “The first step includes five different exfoliating acids: glycolic, lactic, mandelic, phytic acid, and gluconolactone to help remove dead skin cells and improve texture. The second step introduces retinol to smooth fine lines and ectoin to help soothe and hydrate. Rather than relying on exfoliation alone, it combines immediate surface refinement with an ingredient that has established long-term benefits for photoaging.”

Key ingredients: Glycolic, lactic, mandelic, phytic acid, and gluconolactone, retinol, ectoin

Arguably one of the best parts of a facial is leaving with a bouncier, more lifted complexion. Susca calls Ourself’s serum a standout pick thanks to its “deep hydration delivery system,” which she says “provides a deeper lifting and plumping effect while giving the skin a lit-from-within glow.” This system combines dual-weight hyaluronic acid with a booster intended to encourage the skin’s natural production of the ingredient, and an “HA protector” designed to help it stay in the skin for longer. The formula also contains bioactive peptides, said to stimulate collagen and elastin production, and brightening vitamin C and niacinamide.

Additionally, its patented delivery technology targets specific areas of the skin for the most visible impact. In two-week, company-sponsored clinical trials, “this serum has been proven to volumize areas that are losing depth, smooth fine lines, and improve tone with consistent use,” Susca notes.

Key ingredients: Bioactive peptides, HA+ complex, vitamin C, niacinamide, patented tiered-release vesicle technology

For a quick, facial-like reset, ELLE beauty commerce editor Nerisha Penrose swears by this multitasking Korean toner mist, formulated to nourish and calm skin, minimize the appearance of pores, and even out tone.

“I stay away from most buzzy skin care because I’m on a derm-prescribed plan to help erase acne breakouts and post-acne scarring. On the nights when I’m not using my retinol or topical antibiotics, I’m generously spritzing my skin with this deeply hydrating mist,” says Penrose. “The gentle formula combines soothing botanicals and antioxidants that deliver moisture, relief, and barrier strength over time. By the time I wake up, I have the most supple, softest, radiant skin.”

Key ingredients: Rose water, lactobacillus ferment, betaine, melin seed extract, ivy seed extract

“This serum is a fantastic example of exfoliation and hydration working beautifully together, and is one of the best options for dry, mature skin,” says Dr. Ugwu-Dike. “It contains 10 percent lactic acid, which helps loosen the bond between dead skin cells to improve surface texture. But what really makes this formula impactful is the inclusion of ceramides, hyaluronic acid, and glycerin, which help support moisture retention.”

Key ingredients: Lactic acid, ceramides, hyaluronic acid, glycerin

“You want a balanced mix of actives and barrier support,” says Dr. Cheung. “For exfoliation, look for AHAs (lactic, glycolic), BHAs (salicylic acid), or enzymes. For brightening, look for vitamin C, niacinamide, or tranexamic acid. For hydration and barrier support, you want hyaluronic acid, glycerin, and ceramides.”

“If you’re oily or prone to acne, go for BHAs or a combination of exfoliants,” she continues. “If you’re a dry or sensitive type, go for lactic acid or enzymes with more hydration.”

Dr. Ugwu-Dike adds: “Alpha hydroxy acids are some of my favorite ingredients when it comes to achieving that immediate glow. Glycolic acid has a small molecular size, which makes it really effective for treating photo damage and uneven texture. Lactic acid offers both exfoliating and humectant properties, which makes it excellent for somebody whose skin is also dehydrated.”

All our experts agree that it’s best to look for options with multiple active ingredients at lower, “more tolerable” percentages, especially if you have reactive skin. “High-acid concentrations can cause inflammation, which can trigger post-inflammatory hyperpigmentation that can lead to dark marks and skin scarring,” warns Dr. Ugwu-Dike.

Resist the urge to overdo it, Dr. Cheung advises. “Focus on using these with purpose, not just piling on more products. Apply after cleansing, starting once or twice a week, then increasing as tolerated. Don’t stack multiple strong actives the same night to avoid irritation.”

“Hydration is the important finishing touch,” adds Dr. Ugwu-Dike. “I love pairing an exfoliating treatment with a rich, non-irritating moisturizer because it helps create that smooth, glass-like finish people associate with facials.”

As with any skin care product, she notes, the best results come with consistency.

Dr. Jessie Cheung is a board-certified dermatologist with practices in Chicago, Illinois, and New York City.

Samantha Susca is an esthetician and founder of Refinery4 in New York City.

Dr. Pearl Ugwu-Dike is a NYC-based board-certified dermatologist.

Including easy-to-divide gift sets for extra savings.

Big-ticket beauty gifts like a Dyson hair tool or an LED mask may get all the attention during the holidays, but some of the most coveted presents come in small packages—aka stocking stuffers. As a beauty editor, my favorite gifts to give (and receive...hint, hint) are the little treasures I can toss in my purse and reach for all day. Consider this your expert guide to the best beauty stocking stuffers to stock up on this holiday season.

Think of this list as a mini beauty haul, with plenty of editor-backed goodies they’ll actually use, from pimple patch restocks and luxurious hand creams to travel-friendly picks that can make seat 34F feel like first class. Pro tip: I also included gift sets you can split up to fill multiple stockings and save a few bucks. Most picks are under $50, but I also threw in a few luxe finds for anyone you’re ready to spoil.

Medicube’s latest viral hit is basically made for a stocking. This easy-to-swipe balm stick pairs PDRN, collagen, caffeine, vitamin E, and Volufiline to hydrate and give skin a plumper-looking finish wherever they want it, from under the eyes to smile lines. It’s a fun upgrade to their usual eye patch routine—and one they can use on the go.

Our editors—along with the rest of the internet—got hooked on Eos’ Vanilla Cashmere line. The Shea Better body lotion gives winter skin a serious hit of hydration without feeling heavy, and the scent is so good. While the classic body lotion is always an old faithful, why not gift them something with a little extra glam like this holiday edition shimmery version? It’s the same nourishing formula, but with a golden, pearlescent finish for glowy skin.

Another useful beauty stocking stuffer? Dae’s mascara-inspired finishing wand will tame flyaways and frizz for a polished look. The styling cream gives hair flexible hold without leaving it crunchy or stiff. Plus, it’s convenient to carry in a handbag so they can touch up whenever, wherever.

I’ll never say no to more hydrating lippies—and the scents on my personal wish list? Summer Fridays’ vanilla beige, hot cocoa, and brown sugar. Plus, we’ve found that despite its compact size, it lasts for months.

These hydrogel masks are one of the most viral products for achieving an overnight glow—and our editors can confirm they’re worth the obsession. Ingredients like hyaluronic acid, niacinamide, and collagen infuse your skin with hydration and brighten for that glass skin effect. Beauty editor Beth Gillette says it leaves her with “the smoothest skin ever.”

A Cosmo Holy Grail Beauty Award winner, Cyklar’s Perfume Oil is the perfect purse-sized pick for a quick scent refresh on the go. “The scent is so warm, rich, and creamy without being sickly sweet or smelling artificial,” says senior director of editorial operations, Danielle Colin-Thome. “I couldn’t wait to finish testing the other perfume oils on my list so I could go back to using this every day.”

Winter dryness has me reaching for this hydrating mist on repeat, making it a useful addition to their stocking. My skin looks naturally dewy with or without makeup.

Between the delicious scents and plush, whipped texture, this body butter has our editors hooked.

“There’s something magical about this body butter...It beautifully melts into skin and feels weightless,” says contributor Mary Honkus. “The thickness is just right, and the scents are to die for.” It comes with three travel-size pouches so you can tuck one into a stocking or split them among your besties.

Okay, okay. The price on this one isn’t *exactly* stocking stuffer-friendly—but for the skincare-obsessed person on your list, the Depuffi is a little luxury that is totally worth the splurge. It offers hot and cool therapy with six temperature settings to help soothe facial tension and de-puff. “The shape fits the face perfectly, really getting in on all the contours and curves of my cheeks and jawline,” says assistant beauty editor Jasmine Hyman in her review. “The cooling setting is perfect to close out the facial by reducing post-suction redness and providing some extra depuffing.”

Hand sanitizer is a cold and flu season essential, but Gemi’s formula feels a touch more elevated than the usual alcohol-scented, ultra-drying kind. It comes in luxe scents like lavender and geranium, green tea and bergamot, and Fuji apple and rose, and it’s formulated with cica, vitamin B5, and green tea to help keep hands feeling hydrated. Get the version with an attached keychain, and it doubles as a cute bag charm.

When my skin needs a reset, I reach for Dr. Dennis Gross Skincare’s Alpha Beta Universal Daily Peel Pads. The two-step treatment helps smooth texture, brighten my complexion, and fade the look of dark spots over time. This set of five is the perfect little pick-me-up for dull winter skin, especially when my skin is craving a deeper exfoliation.

#6806. Here’s What It Takes to Keep a Pool Running During the Winter, According to Experts

Before you dive in, it’s important to understand the risks and expenses involved.

When most people think of backyard swimming pools, relaxing outdoors in the summertime immediately comes to mind. But some homeowners don’t want the swimming season to end when temperatures drop. Fans of cold-water swimming are starting to consider ways to enjoy their pools throughout the winter as a part of an at-home wellness experience.

“Ten years ago, most people didn’t think winter swims were possible, especially in colder climates,” says Karen Larson, cofounder of Soake Pools. “Times have changed because these days, they’re seeing neighbors, friends, and others do it and post the proof on social media.”

The increasing interest in cold-water experiences is part of a broader wellness trend. In American College of Sports Medicine's 2026 Worldwide Fitness Trends report, cold therapies, including cold plunges, cryotherapy, and cold showers, earned the 17th spot among fitness trends for the year, up from number 20 in its 2025 report.

If you’ve previously closed your swimming pool around Labor Day but are interested in making cold-water swimming a part of your daily wellness routine, there’s a lot to keep in mind. Not every existing pool is a good candidate for keeping open for winter swimming, and it’s important to understand the risks and expenses involved. But if you’re curious, here’s what to consider about keeping a pool open year-round.

Why is cold-water swimming becoming more common? There are numerous purported mental and wellness benefits, from athletic recovery to stress relief and better sleep. A 2025 systematic review and meta-analysis published in PLOS ONE found that cold-water immersion led to a reduction in stress for 12 hours afterward as well as improvements in sleep quality and overall quality of life.

“Winter swimming often creates a time where friends and family can come together without distractions,” adds Larson.

That said, while swimming during the colder months has its perks, there are also several risks to keep in mind. A 2020 review in the International Journal of Environmental Research and Public Health found that cold-water immersion can trigger an immediate shock response, leading to involuntary gasping, hyperventilation, and a rapid increase in heart rate and blood pressure. These reactions can make it difficult to control your breathing and increase your risk of drowning. Cold temps can also impair your muscle strength and nerve function, making it challenging to swim safely.

It’s a good idea to acclimate to the cold water gradually and avoid prolonged exposure. You’ll also want to make sure there’s someone else home while you take your cold-water plunge in the pool.

In addition, if you have underlying conditions like heart disease, consult your doctor before all else, as the cold water may place additional strain on your heart.

If you’re trying to consider whether your pool is a good candidate to keep open during the colder months, these are the things to look into.

The cost of keeping a swimming pool open for winter swimming will depend on your location, size, desired water temperature, and the type of heater you use.

“Routine pool maintenance generally remains about the same year-round, although chemical consumption may decrease depending on how frequently the pool is used,” explains Jim Eisch, Jr., vice president of operations at Pinch A Penny Pool Patio Spa. “The biggest expense to consider in the winter is heating the pool.”

For this reason, prospective winter swimmers may want to consider an upgrade to their heating system. Instead of using pricey natural gas heating or a traditional heat pump, Eisch says that inverter technology is one of the most affordable ways to maintain a swimmable pool temperature year-round.

For example, if you live in Florida and have a 10,000-gallon swimming pool, Eisch estimates your annual heating costs will be $2,467 with a natural gas heater, $741 with a traditional heat pump, and $434 for a heat/cool pump that uses inverter technology.

As aforementioned, the goal with wintertime swimming is not to be soaking in bathwater-like temperatures while it’s freezing outside. For safety purposes, winter swims are quick, and the heating system is to keep your chlorinated pool water well above the 19-degree Fahrenheit freezing point.

Unsurprisingly, a standard 14-by-28-foot swimming pool is going to be one of the hardest to use effectively year-round, unless you live in a region with a mild wintertime climate.

“You can technically use a large pool year-round, but it’s difficult to cover all its surface area well enough to hold in the heat, so heating bills can climb fast,” says Larson.

Therefore, smaller sizes like a 10-by-16-foot cocktail pool or plunge pool are better candidates for keeping open. Dedicated winter swimmers should also invest in an easy on-and-off cover—or a motorized auto cover—for added protection.

Regular pool cleaning and maintenance are essential, and this upkeep over the winter is no exception.

“Check the filtration system regularly to make sure it’s circulating smoothly, monitor the water chemistry, and plan for power outages—because there’s a good chance they will happen,” Larson explains. For this reason, you should also invest in a generator that can keep the pump running if the power goes out.

Safe pool access is just as important as any other aspect of the pool’s design. That’s why a nonslip surface, excellent drainage, and ample lighting are key.

“Your design should also provide a clear path from the house to the water,” says Neha Gupta, interior designer and founder at NU Curations.

Especially in the wintertime when ice and snow are a factor in your region, make sure you have a safe and smooth exit plan for getting out of the water, bundled up, and into your warm home without any obstacles. And then, of course, remember to cover the pool back up to keep it protected and ready for your next plunge.

#6803. Bob Dylan Dressed Like Timothée Chalamet to Meet the Pope

Today, millions of Americans awoke to social media feeds awash with images of and commentary about a landmark event that seemed nigh-impossible a mere 24 hours earlier. I speak, of course, of this image:

As the nation began to digest the results of a historic election that seemed to herald the arrival of a new America, two of our very best Americans met for a private audience on the other side of the Atlantic: Bob Dylan, the Great American artist, and Pope Leo XIV, the first American Pope. Dylan is in the midst of yet another lengthy European tour—his strongest in some number of years, judging by recent bootleg tapes. On November 2, he played a show at Milan’s Unipol Dome, then jetted over to Rome ahead of a November 5 performance at the ​​Palazzo dello Sport. What better way to kill an off-day than a quick chat with the Vicar of Christ?

It wasn’t the first time Bob met a Pope, as some pointed out. In 1997, he performed for John Paul II at the World Eucharistic Congress in Bologna, donning a dapper Western suit and a fine Stetson for the occasion. He and JP2 made for a bit of an odd couple, the mysterious American gunslinger and the seemingly-nonplussed Polish holy man.

Dylan has somewhat more in common with Pope Leo, a.k.a Robert Francis Prevost, a fellow Midwesterner. But even if the two men hail from similar geography, the sight of them together under the bright fluorescent lights of an anonymous Vatican office looked like the product of a well-crafted AI prompt, if not an outright fever dream. The images were so unexpected, so uncanny, I would’ve been convinced they were fake had they not been published by an official press organ of the Vatican.

Much of the whiplash stemmed from the two men’s appearances. Angel and devil. Spy versus spy. The man in the long black coat and the man in the short white mozzetta. The one liners wrote themselves.

On Wednesday, the Pope wore a clean white cassock and a tidy little zucchetto, with an iron cross hanging down around his neck. In short, he looked like the Pope. I suppose I would say the same about Bob: that he looked like himself. As any good Dylan fan knows, however, the meaning of that phrase has changed radically over the years. Bob’s shifting appearance is almost as notorious as his shifting artistic sensibility. Dust bowl refugee, sharp-suited mod, bohemian poltergeist, whatever this is—the man has worn many hats.

A hoodied Timothée Chalamet, seen with Kylie Jenner, in New York City.

Sometime in the early 1990s, Dylan took a liking to the humble hoodie, a stylistic evolution that intersected neatly with his booze-fueled artistic nadir. The hoodie allowed him to hide in plain sight, even as he continued to take the stage around the world on his Never Ending Tour. It was practical, yes, but it was also a defense mechanism, a way to synthesize his compulsion to perform and his aversion to being seen. That it often looked hard as hell did not hurt. (It should come as little surprise that Timothée Chalamet, who may as well have been born wearing a hoodie, seemed to riff on this era when he was channeling Bob all those months ago.)

In the 21st century, Bob came unstuck from time. On landmark records like “Love And Theft” and Modern Times, Dylan burrowed into an imaginary musical past situated somewhere between the Civil War and the Great Depression. His style shifted to match. In the early aughts, he adopted a full country-western guise, complete with a Lee Van Cleef mustache. In the years that followed, his sartorial inspirations shifted east: a little less cowboy, a little more riverboat gambler, often performing in wide-brimmed hats, long frock coats, and string ties. “Rock and roll Mark Twain” wouldn’t have been an inaccurate descriptor.

Which brings us back to today’s meeting with Pope Leo. On first glance, Dylan’s ensemble is bonkers: western black blouson with contrast stitching along the chest and collar; beneath that, a heavyweight black hoodie zipped to the chest; beneath that, a white collared shirt with several buttons undone, collar loosely drawn together with a polka-dot cravat. The hood is decidedly up, stationed atop a black flat brim cap. In some shots, Bob can even be seen sporting leather gloves and an old-fashioned umbrella, which seems to double as a cane.

Part “Man in Black” sobriety, part rock star debauchery, with a dash of the hypebeast flavor from Timmy’s A Complete Unknown press tour—the man got a damn fit off in Vatican City. There’s no other way to describe it. (It’s a shame Pope Leo left his Rhude jacket back at the Papal Palace.)

Still, it’s a look with roots in Bob’s past, or pasts: the hoodies of the ’90s, the Westernwear of the 2000s, even the polka dots of 1965. No one but Bob would ever dare to pair all these disparate elements, particularly for a private audience with the Bishop of Rome. No one but Bob could.

Someone should come up with a word for that.

#6801. 10 Stylish Sofa Covers to Totally Refresh Your Living Room Before the Holidays

Every item on this page was hand-picked by a House Beautiful editor. We may earn commission on some of the items you choose to buy.

Hide stains, protect upholstery, and add instant polish.

Life at home gets messy with its regular residents, and it gets even crazier when guests come over. Hosting season demands the most of our couches, as they become extra seats for family dinner or makeshift beds for overnight stays. It’s not always feasible to swap out your sofa just because the upholstery has seen better days. That’s where the mighty sofa cover comes in.

Whether you opt for a tightly-fitted silhouette or a looser, blanket-style slipcover, a high-quality sofa cover can totally refresh your space. Just think about it: a dated, yellowing couch suddenly looks fresh and brand new. You can even go bold and experiment with patterned options, without the commitment of buying a whole new piece. Pro tip: patterns are also a great way to hide stains.

There are hundreds of sofa cover options available, so below, our shopping team did the hard part for you. We hunted down nine options for different types of couches, including an editor-tested and approved option. Plus, we chatted with interior designer Tiffany Leigh for tips on styling sofa covers, keeping them clean, and more.

Velvet couches are having a moment, so if you want in on the trend but don't want to toss out your current sofa, enter this sumptuous sofa slipcover. Stretch the base piece to fit around a sofa measuring 72 to 96 inches, then cover three cushions with the included covers. The fabric is extra soft, so you feel like you're sitting on a high-end sofa at a fraction of the price. "My family used this velvet slipcover to bring a dated, faded blue sofa back to life in a trendy ivory velvet that looked like it could be at home in any furniture showroom," Associate Shopping Editor Janae McKenzie says. "Even better: it was so soft against my skin that I fell asleep on it during movie night more times than I'm proud of."

Material: Velvet | Colors: 23 | Care: Machine washable

Full-blown tassels might feel like too much texture to add to your everyday sofa, but some subtle fringe is a welcome inclusion. This blanket-style cover drapes easily over a two-three cushion couch, and it’s made of a non-slip fabric designed to stay in place. Even with the rowdiest kids and pets.

Material: Chenille | Colors: 18 | Care: Machine washable

Just because you want to protect your couch doesn’t mean you have to give up dreams of elegant white furniture. This extra-large cream couch cover actually comes in two pieces, so it’s perfect to cover an L-Shaped or U-Shaped sectional. You can protect the chaise arm with ease, and it’s still stain-resistant and machine-washable.

Material: Chenille | Colors: 11 | Care: Machine washable

Sofas are often the center of your family room, which means they can be a high-traffic, mess-prone area. Whether you're worried about pet or kid accidents, or an errant wine spill during book club, this waterproof cover could be a great solution to protect your beloved furniture. The stretchy jacquard fabric is leakproof and fits snug to your cushions and frame.

Material: Polyester-spandex | Colors: 16 | Care: Machine washable

Want to add trendy bouclé upholstery to your home but are hesitant to commit to it 24/7? This slipcover offers the best of both worlds. The fitted fabric makes it appear as though you bought the sofa in this style, but you can easily swap it out when you want a different look or feel. It's all in one piece for your sofa's frame, so you can still add the throw pillows of your choice.

Material: Polyester-spandex | Colors: One | Care: Machine washable

This couch cover is basically your favorite waffle blanket, but it covers the entire sofa. The linen is stonewashed, so it's already soft from the first time you sit on it. We love the neutral and earthy tones it's available in, especially this cinnamon color. If you're unsure whether you'll love it, take advantage of the 30-day trial period.

Material: Cotton-linen blend | Colors: Two | Care: Machine washable

The stretchy spandex of this sofa cover makes it a great choice for an inexpensive, colorful refresh. The textured jacquard fabric comes in seven sizes and a wide range of 30 colors, so you're sure to find something that suits your sofa and style. It's also machine washable, so feel free to enjoy a few wine nights on your sofa, especially if you opt for one of the darker colors.

Material: Polyester-spandex | Colors: 30 | Care: Machine washable

For a much more casual look (and application process), this geometrical sofa cover fits like a big textured blanket, so it'll avoid pooling on one end of the sofa. Plus, it can be used for several purposes: it's a great picnic blanket whenever you decide to change up the look of your sofa. It's bordered with adorable tassels, and the chenille fabric is also durable enough to withstand your furry friends.

Material: Chenille | Colors: 48 | Care: Machine washable

If the idea of investing a small fortune in a white couch sounds like a risky idea, opt for a white sofa slipcover instead. This blanket-like cover is oversized for a luxurious, draping look, and it's available in two light linen shades. It will give your living room that coveted clean, modern feel without triggering your anxiety. The best part? This one is machine washable, so anytime you notice a mark or stain, simply pop it in the wash, and it will be good as new.

Material: Chenille and linen | Colors: Two | Care: Machine washable

If you want something that'll truly protect your sofa from the wrath of your pets, Pottery Barn's pet furniture throw is a no-brainer. Available in three sizes, this lucky find can also be customized in a variety of fabrics, including tweed, bouclé, and chenille, among others. Of course, they're all performance-grade.

Material: Basketweave, Linen, Boucle, Velvet, and more | Colors: 95 | Care: Depends on the fabric material you chose

The size of your sofa cover will depend not only on the size of the sofa or couch you want to protect, but also on the properties of the fabric itself. Leigh says that with a stretchy fabric, you may want a cover with measurements slightly smaller than the dimensions of your sofa for a tighter, more fitted look. For sofa covers with corner ties that allow you to tighten or tie bows, the fabric may have a bit less give, so you'll want to allow for a little extra room in the cover size.

Some styles lend themselves to being covered more effectively than others. Leigh says that sofas with thinner or rolled arms tend to look nicer with a slipcover than those without. You can also choose between having a skirt on your sofa cover or showing off the legs of your furniture, depending on your aesthetic preference. “I like when they go right to the floor because a skirt cover is a much more traditional, covered look,” Leigh says. “If you have a little bit more of a modern style, having a slipcover that stops at the legs can be a fresher, kind of more updated take.”

Natural fabrics, such as chenille or linen, are typically a great choice when selecting a sofa cover fabric. For family rooms or homes with pets, indoor/outdoor fabrics like Crypton that have been treated to repel dirt and debris are safer bets for those wanting something stain-resistant. The stretchiness of the fabric also plays a role in selecting a sofa cover. "If you wanted something a little bit more durable, canvas or cotton would be a really great material on there," Leigh says.

It's always a good idea to pay attention to the care instructions for whatever cover you buy, as fabric care really depends on the individual material. For example, a heavier cotton material can likely withstand more washing. “I would say only wash when you really need to, just like with a really nice sweater,” Leigh says. “Don't wash it every time you wear it because washing breaks down fibers. So, it could reduce the longevity of your sofa cover. Most are designed to be removed and washed. So if and when you feel like 'oh, you know what, it's looking a little bit dingy, it's time,' that's the time to do it.” Additionally, it's essential to consider the size of your cover, as larger ones may necessitate the use of a commercial washing machine.

Additionally, the cover may wrinkle over time, especially with linen, which softens with each wash. “Linen does get a little bit wrinkly, but I think that's kind of the charm of a slipcovered sofa, having that kind of rumpled, you know, 'someone just took a nap here' look,” Leigh says.

“An oatmeal linen slipcover is that very quintessential, relaxed coastal style that you see a lot of slipcovers used in, and I think it's a classic choice that you'll never go wrong with,” Leigh says. Don't run away from patterns either, though—Leigh is seeing a rise in patterned upholstery in the design industry, and it's a chance to push the envelope and have fun with your design choices. “A cover can be a great way to, you know, try out a pattern without necessarily committing to it forever, because if in five years you say, ‘okay, this pattern was fun, but I'm ready for something different,’ you can just change the slipcover as opposed to having to get an all-new sofa,” Leigh says.

At House Beautiful, we are experts in reviewing and buying anything for the home, from mattresses for back pain to reclining sofas. For this story in particular, we asked our staff members to share their favorite sofa cover (if they own one) and spent hours combing the internet, reading hundreds of reviews about the best ones currently available on the market. While we haven't personally tested every product on this list, we've thoroughly outlined the pros and cons of each sofa cover to provide you with all the necessary details before you make a purchase.

For further insight into how to best place sofa covers in your home, we consulted interior designer Tiffany Leigh. Leigh runs her eponymous firm in Ontario, Canada, where her team helps clients bring their dream homes and cottages to life. Since 2019, they have designed approachable and livable interiors that feel welcoming and elevated, focusing on quality craftsmanship, emotional connection, and natural elements.

#6799. Medallion Belts Are Everywhere

Consider it a chicer take on the old Western belt.

Every item on this page was chosen by an ELLE editor. We may earn commission on some of the items you choose to buy.

If the runways are any indication, we’ve all been loving a good, impactful belt. Marc Jacobs loaded models up with 2008-coded chain belts at his most recent show, while McQueen wrapped black leather creations around the waist, which also snaked up to the neck like collar harnesses. Celine presented hulking supersize belts that cemented creative director Michael Rider’s dedication to standout accessorizing for spring/summer 2027. Yet at the center of it all lives the medallion belt. Consider it the most wearable version of the statement belt trend.

The look is an easy way to accessorize instantly. Medallion belts act as a kind of jewelry in this case, with their chunky hardware leading the way. Whether paired with jeans and a T-shirt or slung over a little black dress, they’re both practical and slightly whimsical. Both Dior and Celine have put an emphasis on the medallion silhouette, with chic, polished medal belt buckles engraved with designer logos.

Gilded in gold tones and attached to luscious leather, the designer medallions act as modern cartouches, proudly displaying the brand’s name like a badge. It’s definitely a modern take on logomania. Dior has also used the same medallion design seen on its belts in its beauty products, proving there’s always a desire for cute, shiny things. If the shape feels inherently Marie Antoinette-ified, it’s intentional. Its inspiration draws from the 18th-century Rococo aesthetic of Dior’s couture salons.

Chloé too has released a medallion belt. While it’s less logo-driven, it has all the major hallmarks that make the look both elevated and impactful. Four golden, gleaming horse heads surround a talismanic design. The horse motif is a clear nod to the bohemian style that is closely tied to the fashion house’s history. It also heavily relates to the lineage of the medallion belt itself, which has been around for centuries (from ancient Rome’s military uniforms and beyond) but thrived during the 1970s when Western wear reached a peak obsession. The rounded shapes of modern medallion belts of today also reference the original Native American concho belts, which originated in the American Southwest during the late 1860s and blended Spanish-Mexican aesthetics.

What sets the medallion belt apart from some of the other trending belts of the moment is its inherent ease and practicality. Some brands are even taking things a step further. For Givenchy’s spring/summer 2027 show, creative director Sarah Burton gave the medallion belt a makeover by turning the gilded emblem into a usable compact mirror. These days, the medallion belt is a real rarity in fashion: it’s an opulent staple that’s actually practical, too.

#6797. Matt Damon on the Oscars, Tarantino, and the Roles That Got Away

In the desert, as the song goes, you can remember your name. So it’s fitting that Matt Damon has come here—to a sweltering stretch of inland California near Lancaster—to reflect on his 30-odd-year career as one of the most familiar and bankable faces in Hollywood, and specifically on a year that will go down as one of that career’s most challenging and rewarding passages.

Damon set 2026 off with The Rip, a throwback pulp thriller that reteamed him with his lifetime BFF Ben Affleck. He then went on to dominate the summer to a degree most actors crossing the other side of 55 wouldn’t dream of, with Christopher Nolan’s The Odyssey—a noisy, thrilling, engrossing feat of big-budget moviemaking that wouldn’t have worked without an Odysseus compelling enough to command audiences to take the 20-year journey with him. The role demanded everything in Damon’s toolbox, and then some, but the result was a cultural and commercial run that only Spider-Man himself could top.

Jacket (sold as suit) by Norton & Sons. Shirt by Dolce & Gabbana. Pants by Celine. Cummerbund by Charvet. Pocket square by Budd Shirtmakers. Boots by Tom Ford.

This is rare air, and Damon knows it. Lightning struck once for him, with Good Will Hunting in 1997—he never thought he’d see that happen again, much less 29 years later. If exhaustion is the price of beating those odds, then so be it. Still readjusting to life on dry land, Damon sat down to unpack the most unlikely filmmaking experience of his career—and begin working out where he might want to go next.

This interview has been condensed and edited.

Matt Damon: That is amazing coming from him. Yes, I did hear about it.

Yeah, I think if you talk to any actor my age, any of the usual suspects, they’d probably say the same thing. I think the more you do it, if you’re working with really good people, you’re always improving, you’re getting better. And then you’re living more life and you have your family dynamics, all of your primary relationships kind of fill up your reservoir. I’ve talked to other actors my age about it, Ben included—I think there’s a tendency to push when you’re younger, a little bit, to try to work yourself up, and the older you get, the more available a lot of this stuff is. These very, very, very big emotions are kind of just sitting [near the surface]. And so you can really relax into the work, and it can be very full without being forced.

I think so, yeah. I mean, I’ve never been a part of a movie like The Odyssey that was…. Well, I guess Oppenheimer, to an extent, was somewhat of a phenomenon as well.

My workload was a lot heavier on this one, and everybody’s was, and that was kind of the joy of it. We knew we were the first ones to ever try to do a full film in IMAX [70 mm], and that comes with a whole host of challenges for every single department. We were all, I think, very patient with each other because we knew what was being asked of the other people. So in terms of the acting department—the IMAX load is two and a half minutes or three minutes. And so these big, heavy emotional scenes—you couldn’t play them all the way through. You’d have to cut them up. And the crew was just awesome, very patient with us. It felt like we were explorers, in a way. We got to be the first ones to do it, and that really bonded us.

I never would have expected it. And also, to play a role that’s so physical and, at my age, to even have a role that’s available on a scale like this. I’d always wanted to make a David Lean movie. To have it come at this point in my life, I felt incredibly lucky, not only to be able to do it, but also to be able to contextualize it. I don’t think I would’ve appreciated it as much 20 years ago.

No, I just don’t think I would’ve been able to understand and to hold as much gratitude as I am and as I did throughout the process. It’s all about how you look at things. And in retrospect, yeah, we were probably cold and wet. There was a lot of physical discomfort that was temporary. But because I felt so grateful to be there, I was just so excited. I was just so joyful the whole time that I didn’t really notice any of that.

[Laughs] There are no sure things, man. I think that’s where you get into trouble, being like, Well, this is a surefire hit. I’ve heard that before.

I felt it when I saw it. There is that thing that can happen where you make a movie, and you feel like it’s really good, and it just doesn’t connect, and there’s just nothing you can do about that. But as the audience reactions started to come in and the critical reactions were great as well, it was like, Okay….

Chris [Nolan], the most nervous he is in the entire process, from the very beginning to the very end, is the eve of the film coming out. He’s genuinely nervous. He talks openly about it, because that is the moment that you put it out into the world and you have to live with the reaction. Ultimately, the audience decides. Once it opened and the responses were what they were, I think I felt like, We’re going to be okay. It was a big bet in the sense that it was a big budget. I’m not used to playing in that arena. The numbers that movies have to get to just to break even at that level are just so beyond the movies that I’m known for.

A few of them. But The Martian, which I think is the biggest movie that I’ve ever headlined—I think The Odyssey made three times what that made. And that was a real hit for me. But there’s this other league of these kinds of movies that are in the billions that I’ve just never….

Well, the thing about a role like that is every single day I was paired with an unbelievable scene partner. One day I’d be working with Annie [Hathaway], and then the next day I’d be working with Himesh [Patel]. It’s following this character through all these different stages of his life and people who are close to him. So every day was a different, exciting little challenge, a little puzzle to figure out. I’ve always said that when you’re working with a great actor, they’re so good that they’re good enough for both of you. And it’s almost like this wave comes and you just stand up on your board and ride it. Then you have Samantha Morton, who literally just picks you up and shoulder-carries you.

It’s very hard to come in and do really intense things in a very short time frame. [Morton’s scenes]—that was under a week of shooting. Each day being incredibly intense. And that was what was so incredible about these actors who would come in. They’re under a lot of pressure. Nobody says that, but we all know the deal. I agree. She’s incredible. She’s always been incredible. We had a near-miss working together in 2003—and I got to know her then—in a movie with Heath Ledger. And I hope—it doesn’t always happen right away, but hopefully it’s lodged her back in the minds of people who are making those decisions, because she’s just extraordinary.

That’s the emotional spine of the movie. A lot of that monologue that I have at the end is in voiceover, but I wrote it all out and I had it on my phone and I would just carry it with me off set. By the time I got to work to do the scene with Sam, I hadn’t slept in 24 hours, and by the end of the day it was 36 or whatever. I remember thinking the great thing about this character is he probably didn’t sleep last night. Don’t worry about it. So the weariness was very real for a lot of the movie.

The first time was before The Bourne Identity came out. I had done The Legend of Bagger Vance with Will [Smith] and Charlize [Theron], and that movie didn’t do well. And so I had had these misses. And so there was this stretch where the phone just didn’t ring. The silence was…. It was a real rose-colored lenses coming off.

Well, the other thing was that The Bourne Identity was delayed something like a year. And so the word was, That’s going to be a stinker. But in that time, I went right from [filming] Bourne to Ocean’s Eleven. Then there was this whole period of time where nobody was calling, except for Steven Soderbergh, who called and offered me the movie The Informant! And I was so confused. Marty [Scorsese] goes, “Let’s run this and see how we think it’s going to go.” And Jack took the earpiece out and we rehearsed the scene a few times and Jack was letter-perfect with his dialogue. And so Marty went to get the crew, and as people were coming in I said, “Hey, man, what’s the deal with the earwig? And if he knows [the earpiece is] there, his body stays in that relaxed state. People might think it was laziness. It was the opposite. He was a grinder. He worked really, really hard. There can be hype in the moment, or it can be a zeitgeist thing, but it doesn’t hold up. The goal for me is to make as many of those movies that are around 20 years later. That’s a cool thing. #6794. The Fringe Pieces Fashion Insiders Are Wearing This Fall

Runways say this is the adornment of the season.

Every item on this page was chosen by an ELLE editor. We may earn commission on some of the items you choose to buy.

Fringe never really goes out of style. No matter the season, you can always expect to see the embellishment swaying from the arm of a suede jacket or dangling off a leather bag. So when it comes to trends around the design detail, it’s a mere matter of what form the fringe takes. Lately, fashion’s found itself in a fringe fixation, prompting the trim to move beyond the Western-inspired looks it’s best known for.

Fringe re-emerged on the scene last fall when spring/summer 2026 catwalks from Bottega Veneta, Givenchy, and Chanel showcased the adornment as playful ornamentation for skirts, bags, and even shoes. By the fall/winter 2026 season, others were beginning to chime in with their own takes. There were the boho-inspired bags from Etro, the romantic wispy dresses from Ulla Johnson, and restrained silhouettes from Altuzarra.

Whether you’re looking for a bold statement or a little wink of style, fringe remains a simple way to add flair to any outfit. And right now, there’s a fringed version of just about any wardrobe piece you could think of. Between the classic leather staples and newer avant-garde styles, you’ll find something for every style sensibility.

Do an online search for fringe jackets, and you’ll find no shortage of options to shop. Leather and suede remain tried-and-true materials for this style of outerwear—but now there’s also a plethora of other textiles to shop as well. Opt for Toteme’s viral scarf coat if you’re in the market for a new winter coat, or this tweed number from Etro if you’re looking for a polished piece you can wear to the office.

Nili Lotan Eloi Fringe-Trimmed Suede Jacket

Simon Miller Mabel Vegan Leather Fringe Jacket

If recent fall/winter 2026 runways from Givenchy and Proenza Schouler show us anything, it’s that fringe dresses are reaching new heights. The trim is an especially pretty touch to formalwear and event dresses, providing playful movement with every step to even the simplest silhouettes.

Cara Cara Troy Floral-Print Fringe-Trimmed Cotton-Blend Jersey Midi Dress

Ciebon Nella Asymmetric Fringe Midi Dress

Cult Gaia Noosha Fringed Silk Halterneck Maxi Dress

Just like dresses, fringe skirts are experiencing a similarly sophisticated evolution. Lately, the style has favored sleek satin fringe to create a distinct piece that will immediately elevate anything it’s paired with.

Bottega Veneta Fringed Knitted Silk Midi Skirt

Alaïa Tassle Fringed Asymmetric Wool-Gabardine Midi Skirt

Anna Sui Asymmetric Floral-Flock Fringe-Trimmed Crepe Midi Skirt

The sky’s the limit when it comes to fringe bags these days. There’s long fringe and short fringe. There’s standard leather and suede trim that adds a timeless flair, or more dramatic confections made of sequins, beads, or feathers. With beaded tassel bags on the rise, it makes sense that fringe would take similar cues for an eclectic flourish.

Fendi Croissant Fringed Calf Hair Shoulder Bag

Nili Lotan Asher Fringed-Trimmed Suede Shoulder Bag

After Givenchy debuted a pair of bold fringed mules as part of its spring/summer 2026 collection, fringe exploded onto shoes—heels in particular—in a big way. These Boudoir mules, as they came to be known, introduced a playful take on fringe footwear. Now it’s an ultra-luxe, fashion-forward style that’s perfect for those who never shy away from making a statement.

#6793. I Tried a Korean Lash Lift. Did It Really Live Up to the Hype?

The buzzy treatment promises lifted, fluttery lashes without extensions. Here are my results.

We may earn commission from links on this page, but we only recommend products we love. Promise.

Confession: I’ll try almost anything in the name of longer, more fluttery lashes. That’s especially true if the thing shortens my makeup routine and gets me out the door a little faster in the morning (read: lets me stay in bed even just a few minutes longer). So I was, of course, very excited when I discovered a beauty treatment that promised to accomplish both: the Korean lash lift.

I’d previously heard some not-so-great things about lash lifts. The chemical solution used during the process—typically ammonium thioglycolate (TGA)—comes with a risk of dryness, breakage, and damage, especially if the lift is performed incorrectly or too frequently. But Korean lash lifts have been gaining serious attention (Pinterest reports that searches for the aesthetic treatment are up more than 400 percent) as a potentially gentler alternative, since they can feature formulas and techniques designed to minimize stress on the lashes.

And as someone with stubbornly straight lashes, I was particularly intrigued. To me, nothing ruins a good makeup day quite like lashes that refuse to cooperate, and trust me, I’ve put in the work to find products that make mine behave. If you’re wondering, after testing dozens of eyelash curlers and mascaras, I’ve landed on my undefeated duo: the Kevyn Aucoin Eyelash Curler and Tarte Tartelette Tubing Mascara. But even those two can’t always convince my lashes to hold a curl all day.

So, when I learned that a Korean lash lift could potentially give me weeks of lifted, fluttery lashes, no curler required, I knew I had to try it. Now that I’ve lived with the results for two months—including through a vacation, a wedding, and an apartment move—I have a lot of thoughts.

So, first things first: A Korean lash lift isn’t the same thing as eyelash extensions. Rather than attaching individual fibers to your natural lashes, the treatment uses chemical solutions to reshape the lashes you already have to give them a lifted, curled appearance. It’s the same basic concept as getting a perm for a whole head of curls, but on a much smaller scale.

That technique is similar to traditional lash lifts; the biggest distinction typically comes down to the process and products used. For example, traditional lash lifts tend to use perming formulas with ammonium thioglycolate (TGA), whereas Korean ones usually use cysteamine hydrochloride. The latter chemical is often touted as a gentler or safer alternative, but the truth of the matter is that “we do not yet have sufficient high-quality comparative clinical studies demonstrating that they consistently produce fewer ocular complications than traditional thioglycolate-based lash lifts,” says ophthalmologist Sheri Rowen, MD.

Korean lash lifts are also glueless, meaning they use balm instead of glue to get them to stick to the shield that makes the lashes stand up and have that classic curl.

“Korean lash lifts are often designed with an emphasis on more controlled processing and conditioning of the lashes, which may reduce some of the dryness and brittleness associated with chemical treatments,” says Dr. Rowen. However, this doesn’t automatically mean it’s better or safer than any traditional lash lift; all that depends on how the perming chemicals are applied.

“My overall recommendation is that patients should not assume a lash lift is safer simply because it is labeled ‘Korean,’ ‘gentle,’ or ‘conditioning,’” says Dr. Rowen. “The most important considerations are the ingredients, proper application, careful protection of the ocular surface, and avoiding excessive or repeated chemical processing.”

Still, if the treatment is done well, you can expect a natural-looking lift that makes your existing lashes appear longer, more separated, and more defined without the need for extensions.

For my appointment, I visited Two of a Kind, a lash and brow studio in Santa Monica that offers lash lifts, specifically Korean and what their team calls “hybrid,” meaning they use techniques from both methods to customize the results. The entire treatment took about 40 minutes, although my lash technician mentioned that she’s particularly quick. If you’re planning an appointment, I’d budget closer to an hour or potentially longer, depending on your technician and the specific service.

It was my first time ever getting a lash lift, so I didn’t have anything to compare it to. But Two of a Kind’s founder Jordan Feise told me another difference between the traditional and Korean methods: The former uses one shield that shapes the lashes throughout the appointment. The latter uses two shields, always starting with a flat shield (to straighten the lashes and get closer to the root for more lift, Feise explains), then swapping in a curved shield (to lock in the shape and create a curl, she adds). By using two shields, it separates the softening step and the shaping step, which Feise says gives the technician more control over how your lashes ultimately look. “Using two shields during a lash lift allows us to customize the shape of the lashes during the treatment for a more lifted, natural-looking result,” says Feise. “Together, they give us more control over the final result, helping create a beautiful lift without over-curling the lashes.”

Here’s how the appointment went for me: I laid down and my lash tech cleansed my lashes, removing any makeup, product residue, and oil to prep them for treatment. Then, the flat shield was applied to my lid along the upper lash line. She also made sure to separate my lower lashes from my upper ones. Next, the lifting begins. The initial lift is done using balm and the flat shield, which is a thin, flat pad (instead of a curved rod you’d see with a traditional lash lift). This straightens and lifts the lashes. After processing, the tech switched to that traditional curved lift shield to shape and curl. More processing, then neutralizing the formula (to make sure my eyes/contacts wouldn’t sting after), and plenty of conditioning, and I was all set.

During the appointment, I did what any beauty editor would do: I asked approximately a million questions.

How long would my results last? Around two months, she told me. Could I wear mascara and eye shadow afterward? Absolutely, after the initial 24-hour aftercare period. What about getting my lashes wet? Also fine after 24 hours. And would I have to do anything special to maintain the results?

Not really. She recommended applying a lash conditioner a few times during the first couple of weeks to keep the hairs soft and supple. (Full disclosure: I was a bad patient and only remembered to use it once. I still had great results.)

Basically, after the first 24 hours, I could go back to my normal routine—showering, washing my face, wearing eye makeup, and all—without worrying about ruining my lashes. “Even if I sleep on my face?” I asked. Yep, even then.

I have to admit, I was skeptical. The idea that my lashes could stay perfectly curled through weeks of sleeping, showering, and generally living my life seemed a little too good to be true, honestly. But I was very excited to find out.

Spoiler alert: I was so, so wrong to doubt.

For two months straight, my lashes looked unbelievably long, lifted, and curled, yet still felt soft and looked completely natural. And the best part? I didn’t have to do much of anything to keep them that way.

In fact, I ended up putting my new lashes through what I can only describe as an endurance test. First, there was my birthday trip to Hawaii, where I spent every day swimming in the ocean. Then came a wedding, where plenty of happy tears were shed. Throw in more travel, moving apartments, and a whole lot of stress-induced eye rubbing, and let’s just say I wasn’t exactly treating my lashes like delicate little flowers. Yet, through all of it, they kept their curl.

Initially, I skipped mascara altogether because my lashes looked so good on their own. But because I hadn’t paired my lift with a lash tint—a popular add-on that darkens your lashes—I eventually started incorporating mascara back into my routine for a little extra definition.

The one thing that stayed the same throughout the months was that I no longer needed my eyelash curler. Like, at all. Instead of spending time trying to convince my lashes to cooperate, I could simply run a clean spoolie through them to separate each lash, swipe on a little mascara, and head out the door. A dream come true.

And when I didn’t feel like wearing makeup, a little tinted sunscreen or moisturizer was all I needed to feel put together because my lashes already looked like I’d spent time on them. You know that TikTok trend that’s all about the high-maintenance things we do to stay low-maintenance? Yeah, a Korean lash lift falls squarely in that category.

That was probably my favorite part of it all: The results were noticeable without looking done. Of course, I didn’t have the dramatic, obviously enhanced look of extensions, but my natural lashes had enough lift and definition to make my eyes look more awake and fluttery. It was effortless, understated glam, which is exactly my go-to for my everyday makeup.

By the three-month mark, my lashes had gradually returned to their natural (read: stubby and stick-straight) state. But I was very happy to notice zero brittleness, unusual fallout, or other obvious signs of damage. A win!

That would be a resounding yes. After experiencing nearly three happy months with my Korean lash lift, I can confidently say that it’s one of the most worthwhile beauty treatments I’ve tried in a long time. I absolutely loved the look, the experience, all of it.

All this is coming from someone whose job is to constantly test new products and treatments in the name of beauty journalism. Plenty of them deliver impressive results, but far fewer actually make my everyday life easier. And even fewer genuinely excite me. This one did all three.

I loved how natural my lashes looked, how well the curl held up through trials and tribulations, and how little maintenance was required. But what really sold me was the convenience. Being able to wake up with lashes that already looked lifted and fluttery—and shave several minutes off my makeup routine in the process—was something I appreciated every single morning. It just made me feel so much more confident. One thing to note: It can get pricey. At Two of a Kind Brows, one appointment will set you back $120 for a lift and $160 for a lift and tint.

Would I recommend a Korean lash lift? I’d say it’s absolutely worth it, provided you go to a qualified professional and don’t overdo it by getting lash lifts too often. But once you’ve tried one, you won’t look back.

Catharine Malzahn is a contributing beauty writer at Cosmo. She’s covered all things skincare, makeup, haircare, and nails and has tested so many products and treatments that she’s lost count.

Catharine Malzahn is a contributing beauty writer at Cosmopolitan and was previously the beauty assistant at Good Housekeeping, Woman's Day, and Prevention.

#6792. Kim Kardashian’s Morning Show Look Is a Vintage Paco Rabanne Pastille Party Dress

Every product on this page was chosen by a Harper's BAZAAR editor. We may earn commission on some of the items you choose to buy.

Good morning, Kim Kardashian! Starting off a day of press appointments in New York City, the reality star-turned-actor joined her fellow All’s Fair costars on Good Morning America to promote the legal drama’s second season. And while most of us need a cup of coffee (or two) to get ourselves dressed and out the door, she woke up and slipped straight into a vintage Paco Rabanne party dress.

The look, styled by Law Roach, was an intricate peach gown pulled from the Spring/Summer 1989 couture collection. The top was crafted from hundreds of metal discs, which were stitched together to create a one-shoulder silhouette with a side cutout, making for an asymmetrical, backless piece of armor. From the waist, a long silk-crepe skirt floated to the ankle, where it was met by little heeled sandals with clear PVC straps.

The piece of history was sourced by Maison Vintage Virtuoso, a Paris-based archival studio focused on couture, and was reportedly introduced to Kardashian’s team four months ago. (The same ensemble recently sold for nearly $11,500 on 1st Dibs.)

On GMA, Kardashian shared several candid stories from her time filming All’s Fair, and even revealed that she thought Sarah Paulson’s lower-register on-camera voice was her real voice until just a few weeks ago. Despite this confession, the costars were some of the closest on set, and often made one another break character. “They made Sarah and I one time get up and take a walk around the building because they said we needed to get it together,” the Skims founder told the talk show. “We were laughing so hard.”

Kardashian, who later changed into a sheer knit minidress from Dolce and Gabbana’s Autumn/Winter 1997 collection, has curated a press tour wardrobe full of custom gowns (Ashi Studio), vintage pieces (Todd Oldham), and standout couture looks (Schiaparelli).

#6791. Darian Mensah Might Be the Richest Player in College Football. But He’s Still Going to Class

A decade ago, an interview with the quarterback of the unbeaten, top-ranked team in college football might have involved the player, the reporter, and the team’s sports information director. Maybe the player’s dad stood nearby, keeping guard. But when I talked to Darian Mensah on the Sunday before Halloween, there were five other people on the call, plus a few more sitting in the room with the Miami Hurricanes’ smooth but press-shy signal-caller.

Mensah is the most modern sort of college star, a two-time transfer now at his third school who has navigated a bevy of NIL deals. “I’ve got a great group of people who I think truly want to see me win,” he tells me.

The most notable among them is Malachi Toney, the sophomore receiver who caught 16 balls from Mensah the day before we spoke. By throwing tons of on-target passes, Mensah is comfortably pacing to set college football’s single-season record for completion percentage. As the Canes get ready to travel to South Bend to face No. 4 Notre Dame this weekend, the 21-year-old Heisman Trophy frontrunner is at 80.7 percent, several points clear of second place all-time.

At first glance, Mensah has a simple job: just throw the ball to Toney, who has unparalleled open-field maneuverability. In a 52-point outing against Pittsburgh last month, the two accounted for 194 yards and three way-too-easy scores. “I mean, on the first touchdown, I gave a little signal to Mali,” Mensah recalls. “You can see there's only one guy over the pod of three guys.” The film confirms it: Pitt didn’t put enough defenders near Toney, and Mensah identified it. “You got to keep going to it,” he says.

Mensah loves talking football, though he’s just as happy to get in-depth about how chaotic his life is right now. Mensah is trying to deliver Miami back to its glory days as he manages a variety of commercial arrangements, prepares for his professional future, and, yes, even goes to class, contrary to popular ideas about the NCAA football player experience. “I have to go to class,” he confesses. “Transferring [two] times kind of messed with my credits.” He has three classes per day, on Tuesdays and Thursdays, and has had to keep himself eligible at Tulane (which “set the standard for me”), Duke (“probably even a little bit harder”) and now Miami: “Balancing that, school and football, was tough. But I think it set me up for where I'm at now, where maybe it's not as rigorous as far as academics go.”

Mensah gets particularly excited to discuss fashion, which I bring up because most athletes who sit for GQ have at least a moderate enthusiasm for clothes. Mensah, for what it’s worth, is wearing a cropped Adidas T-shirt—the brand is one of his many partners, alongside Dr Pepper and Sling TV. Miami has a roughly $50 million roster, one of the five biggest budgets in the sport. And Mensah, as the team’s star quarterback, is probably its top earner. But I wondered, more specifically, how much money Mensah is set to earn this year between football and his various NIL agreements. “I don’t know,” he demures. “As much as God allows me to.”

Market rate for a Power 4 starting QB is in the low to mid-seven figures, and Mensah is almost certainly on the high end of that spectrum. I’m not interested in pocket-watching, but just a few weeks ago, the United States did pass a bill that would cap how much someone like Mensah can make. The “Protect College Sports Act,” a bill developed by Sen. Ted Cruz and his Democratic counterpart, Maria Cantwell, may come up for a House vote in the upcoming lame-duck session of Congress. (It passed the Senate with a bipartisan array of 77 votes.) The bill would cap school pay to athletes at about $50 million per university, essentially freezing the market right where Miami’s football team currently stands.

The bill’s backers, including seven-time National Champion Nick Saban, have argued that college football player pay is out of control and endangers the integrity of college sports writ large. Essentially, the bill is coming for Mensah’s money, more than practically anyone else among the hundreds of thousands of NCAA athletes. So how does that sit with him?

“I grew up in a single-parent household, and my mom providing for all my siblings was not easy,” he explains. “So to be able to take care of my family in a way that I wasn't able to before has only been a blessing. I don't really know what to say about that other than I'm blessed to be in the position I'm in.”

Mensah doesn’t preoccupy himself with the weight of Miami football's illustrious tradition. He knows the program was “like a dynasty and a powerhouse back then,” and he’s gotten to meet plenty of legends of The U. “Me and the guys always strive to follow in their footsteps,” he says. “But yeah, I was born in 2005...”

In his relatively short life, Mensah has packed in a lot. After playing high school ball in Santa Maria, California, he started his college career as a three-star true freshman at Tulane in 2024. His only other college offer, he told me, was from FCS Idaho State. He entered the transfer portal to play at Duke in 2025, then reentered after winning the ACC Championship last year. In addition to climbing the economic ladder, Mensah has lived in four cities over the past four years. He’s only 21, but he’s got the palette of a washed-up 32-year-old like me. Maple Street Café in New Orleans, which has a chicken lemon dish that is “some of the most amazing pasta I’ve ever had in my life,” is a standout.

Come 2027, there’s a good chance Mensah will make it five cities in five years. He’s eligible for the NFL draft, and should he declare, he’s expected to be taken early in the first round by one of the league’s many QB-needy teams. But I’m a college football guy at heart, so near the end of our call I ask Mensah what he thinks of the impending 24-team playoff format that’s likely to be instituted next season. "If everything goes to plan," he says, "it won't really concern me." Why not, I ask?
