#6733. Inside the NYC Members' Club Where Republicans and Democrats Party Together

A half-dozen of us are squeezed into a small service elevator, our various colognes clashing with the signature fish-and-rubber scent of Lower Manhattan. The elevator operator blares Chinese ballads, and the young man next to me bobs his head in appreciation. An older man shifts uncomfortably. “Could you actually make it louder?” he snarks. Over the course of one excruciatingly slow ride to the sixth floor, we’re trapped in our private discomfort or pleasure. But we’re all headed to the same place: a midterms watch party at The Bench, a members’ club for people who are into politics but feel like political outsiders. It’s a place, according to its website, where “restless organizers, creatives, misfits, sneakerheads, and policy nerds collide.”

Since its founding two years ago, The Bench has hosted insiders ranging from CBS News editor-in-chief Bari Weiss to New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani. Monthly dues, “just to keep the lights on,” run as little as $50. The space is regularly used for events unaffiliated with The Bench: readings by literary magazines, climate week pop-ups, splashy debates. Michka Bengio, the social club’s owner and co-founder, is an earnest believer in dialogue and, if his programming is any indication, a little bit of a chaos agent. He likes to produce scenarios that underscore political tensions, like when he had Weiss’s The Free Press, co-host a watch party for Mamdani’s 2025 election. According to those who attended, it was a somber evening for the pro-Cuomo crowd, though some of them nevertheless returned to The Bench for this week’s midterms viewing.

On the night of the midterm elections, partygoers had the option of viewing the election results in a spacious, orderly room displaying CNN’s broadcast or in a lounge-y, narrower space screening Fox News’s coverage. In a cozy hallway between the two screens, guests could buy cocktails and popcorn or engage with people whose political views differ from their own—arguably The Bench’s most exclusive offering.

“There’s just a whole splatter of different opinions that come in here,” says David Azoulay, who works with the content agency Fixer Media. “The Free Press, the Manhattan Institute, and then I also get to meet a lot of people who are working in the Democratic space, on the Biden or Kamala Harris campaigns.” Azoulay helped produce events for an “America 250” tour in collaboration with Young America’s Foundation, a conservative youth organization, and has worked with provocateur Ben Shapiro and former Prime Minister Boris Johnson. Though he used to be a registered Democrat, he “grew up” and now identifies as a proud Republican. While Azoulay engaged in a playful back-and-forth with a progressive 21-year-old over what he considers to be the fallacy of socialism, Democratic councilmember Christopher Marte milled about wearing an “I Voted” sticker.

Over the sound of people screaming about the James Talarico-Ken Paxton race, Marte told me he met Bengio 10 years ago through Arena, a New York-based political organization that took off in the wake of the first Trump presidency. “It was all these young people trying to figure out how to get involved in politics. A.O.C. was on the couch, Alessandra Biaggi, all these people who were just curious, post-Trump election,” he says. At the time, Bengio was working as a campaign manager for Michael Basch, a techno-optimistic Democratic NYC mayoral candidate, a gig he secured by asking the only person he knew in politics to introduce them. He’s also worked as a consultant for NBA Africa and managed downtown restaurants like Regina’s Grocery and Miss Lily’s. The Bench is one of four Bengio ventures; he also co-founded the supper club Shtick with his wife, Jacqueline Lobel, and partners with the Hancock Foundation and the Hancock Cafe. On any given event night, he can be found buzzing around the room, excitedly facilitating introductions for his guests.

The son of a Moroccan father and Algerian mother, Bengio grew up in Strasbourg, France. When I ask what motivated him to move to New York in 2001, he deadpans: “Ever heard of the American dream?” More specifically, though, he was jealous of a friend who moved to the States for six months and returned speaking fluent English. “He was the coolest kid,” Bengio says. “And I was like, ‘I want to go to America, too.’ I love basketball,” he says, reorganizing a pile of books so that the edges aligned just so.

Bengio, a first-time voter, is coy about his own politics. Instead, he’s driven by the promise of America “that you can coexist,” he says, and a desire to nurture civil, democratic debate. “I want to be part of the project.”

“We need to really recommit and reaffirm what we mean when we talk about free speech—expression that is unencumbered by political interference in any way, shape, or form,” says Josef Palermo, a former curator at the Kennedy Center who drove up from the nation’s capital to attend this party. Earlier this year, Palermo wrote about the politicization of the Kennedy Center by both the Biden and Trump administrations in an article for The Atlantic. “We need spaces like this in D.C. Everybody’s in their own camps and certain venues are definitely coded one way or the other. I think having something like this would be huge in our nation’s capital.”

Then again, it’s partly New York’s distance from the D.C. swamp that makes talking about politics at The Bench feel cool. The space is decorated with Bengio’s enviable collection of NBA and political memorabilia. (He jokes that he stays up late scrolling vintage sites and bidding on Americana rarities.) Alongside Michael Jordan Wheaties boxes and a slew of rare basketball sneakers, there’s a framed copy of Emile Zola’s 1897 letter to the French youth during the Dreyfus affair, a portable Florida voting booth from the Bush vs. Gore election, a framed paper shift dress from Richard Nixon’s 1968 presidential campaign, and nearly every issue of John F. Kennedy Jr’s George magazine. The one with a Donald Trump cover gets taken down from the wall often, Bengio says, but he always puts it back up.

On Tuesday night, there appeared to be other collectors of rare political merch. Vintage Obama-era crop tops caught my eye, and a speechwriter for a New York City council member waxed poetic about his favorite vinyl record: a collection of John F. Kennedy speeches. Two guys wore t-shirts they designed themselves that cheekily quoted Michigan turncoat Haley Stevens: “Israel cums to me in my dreams.” (One of them requested anonymity, fearful of being cancelled by the Canary Mission, an anonymous organization that tracks critics of Israel.)

A good number of attendees who were professionally invested in the election outcomes couldn’t stop checking their phones. Anthony DiMieri, the man behind Mamdani’s winning social media strategy, told me he’d just come from Brad Lander’s party. Max Altman, the brother of the OpenAI founder Sam, also stopped by. He’s excited about a recent move to New York from Austin, Texas, and if he hadn’t forgotten to request an absentee ballot, he says, he would’ve voted for James Talarico.

As the results turned progressively blue, the room began to clear out. Before leaving, I chatted with Azoulay’s “libertarian friend” Hunt Beaty. In the hallway between broadcasts, Beaty tells me he’s not terribly moved by the midterms. “Everything interesting that is happening in the world right now, to me, is happening outside of politics,” he says. He rejects the libertarian designation and lives by the credo “free minds and free markets,” citing Reason magazine. And yet, Beaty finds that The Bench still has something to offer him.

“It’s fun to be in a room filled with buzzy, interesting people who at least are able to try and talk about ideas, while also being like, ‘Maybe we’re doing coke in the bathroom, too.’ I want there to be a New York City where those things could coexist.”

The Onslaught actress brought ELLE along as she got ready for the meaningful evening.

On Wednesday evening, the Chateau Marmont was in full Hollywood mode as Max Mara gathered friends for a cocktail reception to toast Adria Arjona. The Onslaught actress was named this year’s Women in Film Max Mara Face of the Future, an award recognizing an actress’s achievements in film and television, community contributions, and embodiment of style. (Past honorees include Emily Blunt, Hailee Steinfeld, and Gemma Chan.) With the Women in Film Honors taking place the following night, the gathering offered an intimate start to a larger celebration of women shaping the screen industries.

For what Arjona called an “amazing honor,” she channeled minimal elegance in a sleek black Max Mara gown, its halter neckline bringing a touch of drama to the otherwise understated look. Her longtime partner, Jason Momoa, joined her for the evening, alongside guests including Jessica Alba, Shay Mitchell, Brittany Snow, Zoey Deutch, and Victoria Justice.

The timing feels fitting. Arjona’s recent work in Onslaught, where she plays an army veteran and single mother with PTSD, has expanded her range, and she’ll next appear in The Thomas Crown Affair in March. Away from the set, the Puerto Rican actress has made community work a long-standing commitment, supporting underserved women in downtown Los Angeles for more than a decade and children in Guatemala for 15 years.

From her beauty routine to the final look, plus a car ride filled with friends and family, Arjona brought ELLE behind the scenes as she prepared for the Chateau Marmont celebration.

My other little bestie and love of my life. Oli.

Feel so honored. So thankful to Max Mara and Women in Film for this amazing honor. It was such a fun night. I’ve never felt so special. Thank you.

#6731. The Quiet Rise of DeMellier Handbags

Every product on this page was chosen by a Harper's BAZAAR editor. We may earn commission on some of the items you choose to buy.

Why royals and fashion editors alike love this brand

The Margaux, the Birkin, the Baguette: All are familiar bag styles associated with major fashion houses. Very few handbag-first brands can break through and compete. Enter DeMellier, a British label favored by royals, street-style stars, and fashion editors alike for its understated designs that are big on functionality and eminently reasonable in price.

While many luxury labels are raising prices on handbags, DeMellier’s range hits that sweet spot. Most bag styles ring in between $500 and $600 and capping off well under $1,000. “We believe luxury should be priced with integrity,” says Mireia Llusia-Lindh, creative director and founder of DeMellier London. “This means offering luxury quality and ethical manufacturing without inflated prices by having lower, more reasonable margins than traditional luxury houses.”

Before we hit peak quiet luxury, DeMellier built its foundation on that timeless, minimalist look years ago. (Llusia-Lindh launched Milli Millu in 2010 and rebranded as DeMellier in 2017.) “It’s a philosophy we’ve held since the beginning,” says Llusia-Lindh. “I have always believed in creating pieces that will stand the test of time, avoiding large logos or unnecessary embellishments. For us, luxury is about creating something personal, meaningful, and enduring.”

DeMellier’s New York tote has a minimal, architectural silhouette and is one of the most popular styles from the brand. It’s a bit reminiscent of Celine’s Trapeze, and for Phoebe Philo fans who are nostalgic for the designer’s past artful designs for the label, it fills that void.

The New York tote, which comes in two sizes and different hues and textures, is popular among many fashion editors, including those at Bazaar. “DeMellier has been able to understand that great style and substance are more valuable than trends and fashion. The bags are so chic and provide luxury at a great price point,” says Harper’s Bazaar’s accessories director, Miguel Enamorado.

Plus, the bag can haul a lot: a laptop, a notebook, beauty essentials, headphones, and more. As a New Yorker, I can vouch that it’s aptly named, though it suits any harried commuter’s lifestyle. The long straps are critical when carrying it over a thick jacket or coat. It’s lightweight from the start, so it’s not a drag when filled to the brim. It often prompts compliments and inquiries from friends, curiously asking, “What is that bag?” For me, it instills a sense of confidence and assurance when carrying it.

Earlier this year, DeMellier launched a new counterpart to the New York, called the Brooklyn, which features a similar shape but is equipped with a few design changes, like an interior zipper and a foldover buckle flap.

And for fall, DeMellier introduced new silhouettes like the Sloane (in celebration of its first store opening in London’s Sloane Square) and the Icons 26 collection, a limited-edition capsule where five stylish tastemakers, from Taylor Hill to Romee Strijd, reimagined some of the brand’s signature styles.

DeMellier has a royal fan club too, including Kate Middleton, Meghan Markle, Pippa Middleton, and Princess Beatrice. The Princess of Wales has been spotted carrying the Nano Montreal, a micro toffee-colored bag, on more than one occasion, as well as the small Hudson in mocha suede.

The brand has struck a chord with women searching for elegant, professional handbags that can accompany them during whatever life may throw at them in a given day—an important meeting, a parent-teacher conference, a gym class, a rush to make a bus home, a coffee with friends. Llusia-Lindh emphasizes versatility, noting that she aims for her designs to “transition effortlessly between work, travel, and leisure.” Each bag is named after a metropolitan city, like New York, Tokyo, and Paris, or a more vacation-worthy spot like Capri and Santorini (where you’ll find a range of raffia totes and resort-friendly carryalls).

“DeMellier has demonstrated that they have a true understanding of what the modern handbag customer wants,” shares Marissa Galante Frank, Bloomingdale’s fashion director. “They continue to evolve their silhouettes, update their colorways and use playful new materials like shearling or pony hair. Their handbags have a sophisticated aesthetic at a price point that can appeal to a wide range of customers. Their belted tote styles are ideal for our customers who are looking for chic handbag options that can be worn from day to night.”

Although the brand is based in London, Llusia-Lindh was born in Barcelona and boasts an impressive resumé: an MBA from Harvard Business School and advisory posts at Burberry and LVMH. She is also a mother of three, so she is well-versed in the day-to-day needs of a working woman. “DeMellier reflects my personal values and has always aimed for something more, redefining luxury by putting meaning, female empowerment, ethical craftsmanship, and sustainability at its core,” she says. And at the end of the day, don’t we all just want a bag that gets us from point A to point B and helps us feel powerful getting there?

Below, shop DeMellier’s greatest hits and new fall offerings.

#6730. I Tried the NordicTrack Ultra 1 Reformer—Here Are My Honest Thoughts

Everyone remembers their first time on a reformer, or at least I do. After months of mat Pilates—with a strengthened core and improved flexibility—I thought it was finally time to take things up a notch. Mat sessions, in my naive opinion, were the safer option. Though now I’d argue the right mat class can be significantly tougher, at the time, taking my talents to an actual reformer felt like an uphill athletic battle. Was I ready to handle the challenge of a weighted workout atop a strange machine that could, theoretically, twist me into a pretzel or fling me across the room? With some trepidation, I eventually booked my first reformer class; on my birthday, no less. What better time to try something new?

Fortunately, I quickly learned that reformers are not as intimidating as they seem. Through the instructor’s patient cueing and hands-on adjustments, I quickly got the hang of it. I left the class with an energizing sense of accomplishment, and a Pilates bug that wouldn’t soon die down. Over the next few years, I’ve gone on to take too many classes to count. With my bank account depleted (let’s be real, keeping up with consistent classes is expensive), I wondered if there was a suitable at-home solution. That’s precisely when the NordicTrack Ultra 1 Reformer came across my desk; or rather, was delivered to the World Trade Center’s studio for me to give it a proper test. Read on below to see how the machine works, and if it lives up to a Pilates princess’s expectations.

Launched in May 2026, the Ultra 1 is NordicTrack’s second reformer (the Ultra 1 RX-S launched in 2025); an obvious next chapter for the exercise equipment brand, as Pilates interest continues to grow globally. “We saw a need to create a connected Pilates studio experience that anyone could enjoy at home with a reformer that felt more like high-end furniture than fitness equipment,” Mandy Crane, NordicTrack’s VP, head of brand and product marketing, tells Vogue. “The Ultra 1 Reformer sits at the intersection of excellence in performance and design.”

What you’ll first notice about the Ultra 1 is that it’s a treat to the eyes. Easily one of the most aesthetically pleasing reformers I’ve ever seen (versus reformers I’ve seen in studio and at home), this is crafted with sculpted form, soft edges, and under-side ambient lighting that makes it a statement piece in any room you place it. This, the brand tells me, is precisely what they were going for. “It’s a piece of equipment you don’t feel the need to hide away; you want it to be part of your home,” iFit Pilates product marketing director Yvette McGaffin says. “For me, that’s an important part of wellness through design: creating something that is as considered aesthetically as it is in the way it supports how you move and feel.”

McGaffin, a Pilates instructor and studio owner herself, continues that every design decision serves a purpose, as do the details of the experience itself. “Traditional reformers can involve a learning curve around spring combinations, manual adjustments and the mechanics of the machine. The Ultra 1 brings together studio-grade equipment, push-button resistance, and iFit-guided instruction to make that experience more intuitive and connected.”

Most importantly, NordicTrack wanted the Ultra 1 to suit different body types and experience levels. Though I am not a beginner, I was admittedly a bit hesitant using the machine without a certified instructor present. However, there are a few things in place to eliminate much of the guesswork. Of course, there’s the handy touchscreen that not only offers 75+ streamable reformer Pilates sessions, it also confirms the spring you’re on, flags when it doesn’t match the instructor’s cues, and reinforces the correct footbar position. That way, you can be more certain you’re on the right track. For more experienced users, McGaffin says it’s about expanding what’s possible: “The rear toggles support upper-body work against greater spring resistance, while the Smart Spine can be used as a stable platform for more advanced core, lunge and dynamic, athletic-style exercises,” she says. “

Once the device is in place, getting started is really as simple as plugging it in and toggling the on switch. From there, the lights will illuminate, and you can log in to your iFit account (or make one, obviously) to stream your workout.

The trickiest part of my entire experience, ironically, was situating the springs and footbars. To change the springs, your carriage must be firmly in the home position. If you’re having trouble, learn from me, and ensure the long strap is on the shoulder rest; mine was on the short strap, which pulled the carriage towards the other end of the frame. Once home, you can press the button located near the footbar to activate your desired resistance level. From left to right, you have Blue (33 lbs), Red (44 lbs), and Green (22 lbs); pick one or any combination of the three to your liking or as cued by your workout.

What’s nice, though, is that the spring system is enclosed, meaning you’ll never have to worry about hitting or falling on them throughout your workout. According to McGaffin, this is its Smart Spine framing. “The push-button controls also remove the need to manually change springs, helping simplify setup for people who are new to reformer Pilates and allowing them to focus more on learning the movement.”

The footbars, on the other hand, have four positions available. To change position, gently lift and push or pull to the desired angle. Once locked in place, the footbar position and resistance level will appear in the top right of your screen.

Choosing your workout is genuinely as simple as scrolling through the options, and choosing the right one for you. Certain options, marked by experience level from beginner to advanced, are available as a series, meaning you can do one workout at a time (ideally, per day) for the full effect. Some standouts include Sweat & Sculpt, Powerhouse Performance, and the Aligned Athlete series. Generally, each session lasts about 45 to 50 minutes.

To get warmed up, I started with iFit’s Reformer Essentials program, which further walked me through how to get the most out of the Ultra 1. After that, I took my time looking through the vast library of offerings. Throughout my test, I most enjoyed the Sculpt & Fly series, instructed by McGaffin, to build strength and stamina. While some classes can focus on subtle movements and intensive stretching, this one was much more powerful. It felt like a combination of cardio-meets-Pilates that helped tone, but also break a sweat.

As this class utilizes the jumpboard and Pilates box, with specific exercises catered to the full body, you do move around a lot throughout the duration of a session. That said, because no one was cueing me to the next move or improving my form, I found that I tried to keep my eyes glued to the screen. Fortunately, the screen has a good range of movement; save for when I faced the back of the reformer, I had no issues keeping up.

Overall, I found the Ultra 1 seamless to use. The glide on this thing is incredible—the carriage moves smoothly, and is quite comfortable to exercise on. For reference, I’m 5’2” and did not have any issues whether I was lying down, using the straps, or pushing off the footbar. Sometimes I had trouble locating the straps during pose transitions, but that’s normal for any class. The entire machine weighs about 300 lbs, which is on the heavier side, and it features wood accents and a very stable steel-frame structure. Where weight can be of concern is if you’re moving it around: It’s for sure a two-person job, even to rotate it from one side of the room to another.

The more workouts I completed, the more comfortable I felt with the machine. My biggest piece of advice would be, don’t force yourself to move too quickly—whether that’s pushing yourself to do the most challenging movements or complete the most advanced series. McGaffin offers similar guidance: “Reformer Pilates offers something quite special because it can be both a physical challenge and a chance to switch off from everything else,” she says. “My advice is not to get caught up in how an exercise looks or how much resistance you're using. Stay connected to your breath, move with intention and pay attention to how your body feels. That’s where the real mind-body connection develops.”

#6729. The 45 Best Movies to Watch With Your Parents Without Making It Weird

The family room has been declared an Awkward-Free Zone.

We may earn commission from links on this page, but we only recommend products we love. Promise.

Home for the holidays? Living with your parents again? Welcome to the club... and not the fun kind of club that couldn't even handle you right now, once upon a time.

Let's say you and your roommates (aka mom and dad, maybe grandma and grandpa too) are looking for a quality movie to watch together that won't be filled with awkward scenes or jokes that only you laugh at while the dog side-eyes you from the carpet. It really puts a damper on your weekly Netflix scroll if you aren't careful. Nothing too artsy. Nothing you’ll have to explain. You want something adult, but not that kind of adult.

There's always a risk that family movie night implodes and ends with someone storming out of the room. Committing to the wrong movie is like opting to wear that cute pair of heels that always make your feet hurt even before you've left the Uber―painful and totally avoidable.

From action to comedy to classics, these movies will make your next family movie night more entertaining, less stressful, and an all-around good time. Just because a movie is the dreaded "family-friendly" doesn't mean it has to be boring or, like, for literal children. Swap your stilettos for your slippers, snuggle up on the couch, and start streaming.

You don't need to be a race-car fan (or know much about it in general) to enjoy this 2019 Best Picture nomination. An exhilarating film from both a storyline and videography standpoint, it stars your faves Christian Bale and Matt Damon. Lots of fast cars, personal demons, and some bromance.

This semi-autobiographical rock musical was written by Jonathan Larson before he found success with Rent and, subsequently, died far too young from an aortic dissection. But despite the real life tragedy, the movie is far from a bummer. Directed by Lin-Manuel Miranda and starring Andrew Garfield, it is an absolute joy and can offer your Sound of Music-loving family members a new musical to obsess over.

Don't listen to your older siblings: you're never, I mean never, too old for an animated Disney movie. Moana is something special; it’s a delightful story about embracing your identity and realizing your potential. And the music.

Isn’t it kind of crazy that this is rated PG-13? When a sequel not only lives up to, but also―dare I say―surpasses the first film, it's noteworthy. Meet the Fockers is one of the greatest sequels of all time. You also kind of NEED to watch before the next one, starring Ariana Grande, hits theaters.

Sure, you watched Ocean's Eleven back when it first came out in 2001, or caught the last 30 minutes on a hotel television once or twice. But when's the last time you re-watched it from start to finish? The legendary film about a casino heist is quick, witty, and action-packed. If the glossy crimes don't give you a rush of exhilaration and thrill, then Brad Pitt and George Clooney's dreamy faces sure will.

There's a lot to love about this movie and Ryan Gosling's abs are just six one of 'em. A quick warning, though. If you'd rather avoid a-l-l sex scenes when watching with your parentos, there are a few moments of Emma Stone and Ryan Gosling smooching in bed. And some of the power dynamics are questionable at best.

Next time you're stuck in Indecision Land, propose a fam trip to Middle-earth. Relatives of all ages will get lost in the magical world of Frodo, Gandalf, Gollum, and the whole gang. Even better, suggest a whole Lord of the Rings trilogy marathon―you’ll be set for the entire weekend.

The Family Stone often gets overlooked but it's a very touching story about acceptance and love. Especially good to watch around the holidays, it'll remind your blood relatives that every family has their own chaotic energy, not just yours. Also, not sure if you’ve heard, but there’s a sequel on the way!

Some days just call for a stress-free, aesthetically-pleasing, feel-good movie. Even better if it's about―you guessed it―food. Jon Favreau whips up a delicious film about the restaurant industry and family, but do not put this on the TV on an empty stomach. Actually, it'd be a fun one to make into a TV dinner situation.

You say "I want a heart-racing, invigorating movie." I say "Miracle." Hockey’s gotten randomly popular lately, so why not? It's about the 1980 U.S. men's Olympic hockey team and how they became a microcosm for American patriotism during the Cold War. It also has the greatest pump-up speech in cinematic history. Sometimes I listen to it when I'm feeling down and it makes me feel alive. Don't @ me, just watch.

Suspenseful, captivating, thrilling, and a true story? Argo tells the tale of one of the CIA's greatest top-secret missions that took place during the 1972 Iran Hostage Crisis. Ben Affleck stars in and directed this conversation starter of a film, which was nominated for *seven* Academy Awards and won three—including Best Picture.

An oldie but a goodie with Robin Williams and Nathan Lane. Hilarious at every moment. Once you meet Hank Azaria’s character, Agador Spartacus, you will never be the same. I laugh just thinking about it.

Is Albert Brennaman one of the greatest characters of all time? Probably not but his dance moves will go down in history. IYKYK, and if you don't, watch it.

Courtroom dramas and comedies are guaranteed crowd pleasers. When you've just about had it with your extended fam, turn on this movie and you'll be grateful Vinny isn't a relative. Unless...

If there's one thing guaranteed to please a crowd, it's a Tom-Hanks-and-Meg-Ryan romance. The classic tale of mistaken identity (and, oddly enough, the ins and outs of corporate book-selling) is charming enough that its take on the internet—chat rooms, lol—doesn't even seem annoyingly outdated, it just seems adorable. Set during the holiday season, it earns bonus points for cheer.

It's probably been way too long since anyone in your family sat down to watch the feature that put Matt Damon and Ben Affleck on the map, so why not rectify that together? Good Will Hunting even includes one of dearly departed Robin Williams's finest performances, in addition to wit and heart in equal measure.

The Oscar-nominated documentary might sound too cerebral for holiday consumption—it's about the tumultuous relationship between an artist and his wife—but the final product is touching, funny, and relatable.

An excellent movie series that the whole fam will get into. I mean, you can't go too long without re-watching the legend that is Katniss Everdeen. With two new installments, The Ballad of Songbirds and Snakes and Sunrise on the Reaping, this franchise is expanding in ways that demand more and more marathons.

This award-winning Sundance documentary will effectively cure any desire for your family to overspend on gifts this holiday (it's about one of America's richest families and their major money troubles), while also providing a screamingly funny inside look at a wacky, decadent lifestyle typically seen only on reality television.

Everyone loves Jennifer Lawrence. And Bradley Cooper. And Robert De Niro. And dancing. And sports. And an exciting competition.

James Bond is always a crowd-pleaser, and Daniel Craig's third entry into the ever-expanding 007 canon offers up both action and drama to spare. Plus: Adele.

This 2012 Oscar winner for Best Documentary is a full cinematic experience, and one that just so happens to sound damn good as it goes down. The feature chronicles some of music's most under-appreciated talents (back-up singers), and weaves in inspiring stories with some incredible music. Your entire family will be dancing in no time.

The amazingly talented Lake Bell wrote, directed, and starred in this hilarious 2013 comedy about the weird world of movie voiceover artists. Despite its highly specific subject matter, the film still works as an uproarious story about a gal just trying to make it. Even better? Her dad just happens to be the world's best voiceover guy, so it's got extra family resonance.

Do your parents not quite understand your current lifestyle choices? Introduce them to the incredibly charming (and slightly dunderheaded) Frances Ha. Odds are, they'll feel much better about your direction in life, even as they fall totally in love with the perfect creature that is Greta Gerwig.

There's no better way to follow up You've Got Mail than with yet another Hanks/Ryan pairing. Get out the hankies.

Sure, the Hayley Mills original is a classic, but this modern take on the old "separated at birth" story is funnier and flashier. It also features Lindsay Lohan in her most adorable role ever. Just prepare your most diplomatic answer for when your grandmother inevitably asks you, "What's that cute girl up to these days?"

It's an inspirational sports tale that feels appropriate for the season without actually compelling anyone to take up a new sport during this winter.

If you haven't seen the re-make Annie movie, now is the perfect time to catch up on hard-knock lives, fluffy puppies, and enough good cheer to make the entire family stand up and sing.

Use this time together to catch up on classic features that might have otherwise eluded you, including the kind of stuff that will send your grandparents swooning into their own memories of Audrey Hepburn, Gregory Peck, and the Italy of yesteryear.

It's probably been a minute since you saw the ultimate family bonding feature, and, yes, it's as good as you remember.

This fictionalized making-of-Mary Poppins movie is charming, heartbreaking, and will fill you and your parents' hearts with nostalgia while also teaching you something new about the woman who invented the practically perfect nanny.

Speaking of getting nostalgia shot straight to the heart, Marielle Heller's film about Fred Rogers and a cynical reporter who profiled him is kind of a masterpiece. They’re played by Tom Hanks and Matthew Rhys, respectively. The movie also chips away at toxic masculinity in a subtle way, if you want to come to family movie night with a low-key feminist agenda.

Greta Gerwig's adaptation highlights two of literature's best parents — insert Bob Odenkirk's "my little women" gif here — and revitalizes the classic in a way that will make it fresh for you and your parents.

Nothing says "dad movie" more than watching someone who's good at their job solve a problem. Ridley Scott's The Martian is two hours and twenty-four minutes of just that. Need I say more? It’s also technically a comedy.

Share a little history lesson with your folks. Pride is the story of a group of gay rights activists in 1980s London who go to a mining community to support a worker's strike because they have a common enemy in the cops that target them for harassment. The happy, hopeful ending has "feel-good" written all over it.

Sick of your parents talking about Hamilton to the point where you're pretty sure they don't actually get it? Why not steer them towards another musical that was filmed for a streaming network? Just make sure to have plenty of tissues on hand. You'll need them.

This is a nice and tremendously well-acted indie movie about the employees at a group home and the kids they look after. It also has a cast stacked with some of today's biggest stars. So if you actually like being IMDb for your parents and answering "where do I know them from?" every five minutes to show off your Hollywood trivia skills, this is the perfect movie for your fam.

Alternatively, take a peek into what your parents were like at your age and watch this Boomer (compliment, in this case) classic. Indulge them. It does have a great soundtrack. And since it’s streaming on Tubi, you can introduce them to their next favorite app. Parents love anything that’s free.

It's science fiction, but also a comedy, and accessible for the whole family. You don’t need to know anything about Star Trek or any other science fiction franchise. Galaxy Quest makes fun of Star Trek fans, but in a loving way.

Dads love westerns, and this is a neo-western. There is "brief" "sexuality" in Hell or High Water, so fair warning there... but I think you and your folks can handle it.

This coming-of-age comedy is about a girl who loves Dolly Parton and enters a local beauty pageant in order to get closer to her mother. It's super cute, romantic, a gret way to honor Dolly’s legacy, and will get your toe tapping to boot!

If you must watch a war movie with your parents, you might as well make it a war movie full of cameos from all your crushes to hold your attention. George MacKay! Andrew Scott! Richard Madden! Colin Firth! (It's also a very good movie with engaging action and an emotional plot, you know, if you care.)

Amma Asante’s period drama about a biracial women set to inherit a fortune in 18th century England, is based on a true story. It’ll satisfy your Bridgerton craving without making things awkward. Belle also, hint-hint and nudge-nudge, features a young James Norton and Sam Reid.

Do people still watch this coming-of-age story about four boys in rural West Virginia who learn how to build rockets in the 1960s? They should! Jake Gyllenhaal plays the leader. Laura Dern plays the teacher who believes in him. It’s such a charmer.

This movie offers romance for the women in your family and the opportunity to start listing facts about Superman actor Christopher Reeve for the men. Or maybe your family defies such traditional gender roles, and it’s the opposite or some combination of the two. What you’ll all get is a great movie experience.

#6728. Grandmacore Bags Are the Textural Treat Your Winter Wardrobe Needs

Every item on this page was chosen by an ELLE editor. We may earn commission on some of the items you choose to buy.

Gather your crochet hooks and embroidery hoops and get ready to embrace fashion’s new era of cozy bags. Needlepoint, embroidery, and tapestry are taking over bags far and wide, from chic clutches to big, oversize carryalls, useful totes, and reimagined duffles. The trend kicked off about a year ago when Valentino launched its DeVain bag in November 2025 as part of its pre-fall 2026 collection under Alessandro Michele. With its beaded details, tapestry textiles, and embroidery, the bag is a love letter to a new kind of grandmacore with a dash of boho.

Much like the tassels that we’ve been seeing so much of lately, the grandmacore bag speaks volumes about tactile, touchable joy in an increasingly digital world. It’s reminiscent of a comfy couch with pillows, or a well-worn blanket that’s been passed down by generations. It’s instant, wearable craft.

Valentino isn’t the only one putting a focus on crafty, comfy bags. Just look at Dries Van Noten. One bag from the fall/winter 2026 collection in particular feels perfectly primed for the grandma-centric fashion universe: an east-west duffel-style tote replete with floral tapestry and a large snakeskin-effect patch. It feels like a wearable textural wonder with an inherent vintage sentiment; something that could have been picked up on travels in a foreign land decades ago and passed down through generations.

Elsewhere, Fendi recently reissued 20 archival versions of the Baguette under chief creative officer Maria Grazia Chiuri, most of them collaged in craft. Think: intense zebra-striped beadwork, mirror appliqué, and floral embroidery made by (and inspired by) South Asian craft. The mirror bag, for example, involves 138 hours of handwork with the Mumbai atelier Chanakya International. All of these bags is clear nods to craft in a world where fashion (and many other things) are lightning fast.

The grandma-ification of bags comes at the perfect time, too. Beyond offering a bit of slowed-down, tactile luxury, these kinds of accessories are also the perfect touch for winter and holiday dressing. There are many ways to wear the look. Silky pouches finished with embroidery by Conner Ives or feather-trimmed shoulder bags from Erdem included. Details like fringe and tassels add extra feeling. When all you see is the coat, let the bag do the talking.

#6727. All the Wardrobe Essentials Every Guy Should Own in 2026

When it comes to getting dressed, we often rhapsodize about the virtues of “wardrobe essentials for men” as if everyone knows what we mean. So, let's actually talk about it.

On Maslow's hierarchy of menswear needs, wardrobe essentials might begin the perfect white tee, a killer pair of jeans, and the shoes you can wear with them. But in compiling this list, our goal wasn’t simply to meet your needs—you are, frankly, a grown-ass man, and hopefully have those covered—but more to remind you of the fundamental pieces of menswear that have helped men look hotter and feel better for generations. And in a world of non-stop trends, we need these reminders now more than ever.

In aggregate, our essentials constitute the foundation of a rock-solid men’s basic wardrobe. Below, a highly specific starter pack of everything you’ll want—nay, need—to wear in the year of our lord 2026.

A plain white T-shirt can be worn as an undershirt, standalone with some vintage jeans, or—if you want to get DIY—screen-printed into a work of art. Looking for an indie version no one else has? Check out our guide to the best white tees.

Slim, abbreviated trunks or boxer briefs that keep everything in place are the foundation of every rock-solid wardrobe—whether other people can see ‘em or not. Even if you’re in the minority that’s committed to boxer shorts, it pays to spend a little more on something that’s, you know, holding your balls all day long.

We love the zany knitwear options flooding the internet these days. But if we're honest, there will always be a spot in our closets for a classic crewneck sweater. They're timeless and endlessly style-able, even if you only manage to drape one across your shoulders.

There's a reason that the Levi's 501s is at the very top of our guide to the best men's jeans: it has been, is, and always will be the jeans you come back to again (and again, and again). If you dig your denim light and a little looser, though, Gap's Loose Jeans are a close second. Can't think of what to wear? Here's your answer, seven days a week.

If there’s another theme here, it’s that menswear essentials shouldn’t be unitaskers. They should be useful in a variety of situations, and when it comes to tailoring in particular, the navy blazer is a Swiss Army Knife. It works in almost any situation, from job interviews (with a tie) to weddings (someone else's or your own). Bonus points if you opt for a double-breasted number with strong shoulders, brash peak lapels, and an unmistakable sense of what Italians—and menswear guys—call sprezzatura.

The menswear-sphere admittedly overloaded on loafers, and we’re now seeing a slight shift in the shoe zeitgeist. But that doesn’t take away from the fact that the right pair of loafers can still be the most versatile kicks in your closet. They’ve got more range than Daniel Day-Lewis and can go from casual to dressy to punk in a flash. Wear 'em with socks or without, and count yourself lucky when they get truly worn in—then keep wearing them.

Sure, everyone knows a guy who refuses to wear shorts. But he's overpowered every time by his greatest foes: Those months of the year where, honestly, wearing anything but a short becomes a compromise. Our favorite pairs merge style with practicality, and only look better the more thrashed they get. (Except for the Champion shorts—maybe keep those a little cleaner.)

They may have emerged from the sweaty, stylish world of sportswear, but hoodies have long since transcended their athletic origins. These ones have the stamina to take you from a coffee run to casual Friday at the office (just put it under one of those jean jackets we're always telling you about).

We get that simple sneakers aren’t exactly the type of kicks you lust after on StockX, but there’s no denying the rush of dopamine you get when you break out a fresh pair, or how well they go with literally everything. At less than a Benjamin there's the Converse Chuck Taylor, a mainstay of our sneakers coverage, since, uh, always.

Not ready to take the plunge on a serious diver from Rolex or Omega? You're in luck: Seiko's much-heralded 5 series gives you everything you could want in a dive watch—an automatic movement, a day-date display, water resistance, and a near-indestructible case—at a price that won't require a second mortgage. (If you've got a few more dollars to play around with, Hamilton is no slouch, either.)

Like a plain white tee or simple white crew socks, a white Oxford shirt is a true workhorse. It can take the 9-to-5 like a champ, sharpen up for a fancier occasion, or kick back wide open over your favorite vintage tee. If you only have one shirt with buttons, let it be this.

Remember chinos? The wardrobe staple of preppies and, inexplicably, grandpas everywhere? The pant that taps in when your jeans need a break? The ones that Gap viral-ized in the late-90s? These days chinos are back and bigger than before. The chinos of today are surprisingly familiar and look more like the military-issued pairs of the midcentury—high rise and hella roomy. Some even have a pleat or two. We're all for going wide and pleated, but these both present a happy-ish medium.

While people usually start talking about them in April, sunglasses are a year-round necessity—overcast January skies be damned. They’re relevant whether you’re soaking up the summer rays, trying to cut the wintry glare, or simply trying to navigate life with a little more stealth.

Headwear trends come and go—we see you, crochet knit beanies and Trucker hats—but the baseball cap is eternal. You wear one, your dad wears one, your grandpa wears one. The solution for everything from a bad hair day, to an impromptu work Zoom, to forgetting to pack your sunglasses, they're also just plain cool, whether brand new or a little worn out. Always have been, always will.

Sweatpants should be cozy, sure, but the best of the genre are so much more than mere lazy-Sunday garb. We’ve moved past the calf-gripping elastane-pumped versions that have defined the closets of so many Lulu bros and dudes who have skate decks hung up as art. Instead, sweatpants now should be closer to the originals with a baggier fit and even wide-open hems. Spring for a pair that oozes Rocky-level charm, and they'll become the bed-to-bodega bottoms you can't stop wearing outside of the house, too.

There were a few years where the collective menswear consciousness leaned into “fun socks,” and further away from God. How easily we are led astray… Thankfully, we all now agree that the best socks are really the ones you forget that you're wearing, because they're so quietly consistent and comfortable. And in all of our years of reporting on savvy men's style choices, we've never heard a bad word said against any of the four contenders below.

Sometimes clothes can make you feel like you’re living a movie, and a good trench coat is like you’re aiming for an Oscar. (Those trucker jackets with the sewn-in hoodie are more like Hallmark). It’s the most dramatic garment you can have in your closet, and while wooden top coats are great when it's freezing out, a lighter-weight trench coat works the other nine months of the year—and can be paired with a heavy sweater for the other three. You may not be starring in any blockbusters coming up soon, but, boy, will you look like you're ready to.

In cooler temperatures, a reliable flannel shirt is more than a wardrobe essential: it's a no-brainer. Most versions will be plaid, but all of them should feel substantial enough to double as a light jacket, thanks to their lightweight wool or thick cotton make.

It's hard to think of a jacket more useful, more handsome, more versatile—heck, more all three at once—than the canvas jacket. These days, the original designs still retains their utilitarian charm, but the hammer and nails that used to accompany them have long since been replaced by a cell phone and ear buds. And thanks to fashion's ongoing workwear fixation, there's never been a wider range of luxe designer versions available.

Black derbies can pull through when you need shoes for more formal occasions—and also elevate a quick-and-dirty jeans-and-tee outfit. Dr. Martens are a great entry-level choice, and you'll get a lot more mileage out of the Mono pair, which forgoes the brand's signature yellow stitching for discreet black thread.

When your dress pants are this good—roomy and comfortable, statement-making but versatile—there's no sense in saving them for special occasions. Wear them all the time, with anything, the way you would your jeans.

Belts are often an afterthought, but they really shouldn't be. So don't waist (sorry) the opportunity. Much like cowboy boots, the western belt is riding high in fashion right now—but for this story's purposes, we'd like to guide you back to more classic styles, even if the two belts up top have a certain western flair.

By now, you're probably getting the idea that the name of the game here is versatility. While you could opt for Chelsea boots—the right pair will be able to withstand the elements, and any sideways glances from your office nemesis—you'll feel so much calmer in a pair truly designed to stomping through snowy slush.

We love that iconic North Face puffer as much as the next guy (you know the one we're talking about). But don't let its objectively perfect design distract you from the avalanche of stellar, lesser-known alternatives on the market.

A good duffel bag needs to do only one thing: hold stuff. A great duffel bag, though, needs to check off a few more boxes. It should still carry your clothes, kicks, chargers, toiletries, and everything else in the most space-efficient, easy-to-find way possible. But it should also be designed to outlast your passport—or better yet, you—despite years of being stuffed in an overhead bin and thrown in the trunk of your car. We've tested hundreds of 'em over the years, and the ones below offer all that and more.

#6724. 7 Best Ways to Care for Gray Hair in the Colder Months, From Boosting Hydration to Restoring Shine

Easy tricks to keep silver strands healthy and hydrated when the temperature drops.

Every item on this page was chosen by an ELLE editor. We may earn commission on some of the items you choose to buy.

If red carpets and runways are anything to go by this autumn, silver strands are the trend du jour. Emma Thompson, Olivia Colman, and Sarah Jessica Parker are leading the former camp, each having debuted an elegant gray transformation in recent weeks, while shows such as Lanvin, Akrin, and Andreas Kronthaler for Vivienne Westwood spotlighted gray hair at Paris Fashion Week.

It seems, then, that there’s no better time to embrace gray and silver hair. But for anyone seeking to follow suit, it’s important to note that cooler temperatures can affect the typical upkeep involved. “Cold weather dries out gray hair, making it feel rough, brittle, and more prone to breakage and frizz,” says John Clark, senior colorist at Nicola Clarke salon. “This is because the cold, low-humidity air pulls moisture from the hair, while indoor heating further dries it out.”

Since gray hair indicates a structural change in the hair (as it’s caused by a loss of melanin in the strands), it’s often more prone to dryness, regardless of the weather. Dr. Aamna Adel, founder of Rhute Haircare, explains: “Gray or white hair often has fewer natural lipids and a rougher cuticle, which means it can feel drier and coarser. It also reflects light differently, so it can look dull or wiry.”

She adds that both the texture of the hair and the scalp can change when temperatures drop; flakiness and irritation can be common consequences.

Thankfully, there is a range of easy ways to restore both back into top form. With winter firmly on the horizon, discover the seven swaps and changes you can make to your gray hair routine to best care for it in the weeks ahead.

A healthy scalp will ensure that gray strands are stronger and denser, according to hairstylist and founder of Jo Nova, Joseph Yildiz.

Adds Dr. Adel: “Look for ceramides, fatty acids, shea butter, and panthenol to rebuild the lipid barrier; niacinamide to support scalp health; and antioxidants like vitamin E, stem cell extracts, and green tea extract to protect against oxidative stress, which accelerates graying and dryness. Amino acids and peptides can also help strengthen the hair shaft over time.”

As gray hair naturally feels coarser, the last thing you want is to strip it with shampoos that contain harsh sulfates. Opt for hydrating formulas or cleansing conditioners, and while the hair is damp, apply a leave-in conditioner.

Incorporate a silver shampoo and conditioner once a week. “It dulls any yellow or brassy tones and helps reflect the light, making hair look shiny and glossy,” says Clark.

Alongside this, a clarifying formula used once every two weeks is useful, too, especially if you tend to use a lot of styling products. “It will lightly cleanse any product buildup or mineral deposits in the hair. Sometimes white hair can appear yellow, and this solves that,” says Jo Cockle at John Frieda Salon. Always follow with a bond-building and moisturizing hair mask to keep it strong and soft.

Philip Kingsley Pure Blonde/Silver Shampoo

K18 Full-Size Leave-In Molecular Repair Hair Mask

Avoid stepping outside into the cold right after air-drying your hair. “This can be incredibly damaging to hair that is already prone to dryness. The water in your hair can expand in freezing temperatures, which can lift the hair’s cuticle and lead to split ends,” says Hollie Rose Clarke, hairstylist and Living Proof ambassador.

Instead, she recommends using a hydrating product to help keep hair soft and conditioned while air-drying. Clarke is a fan of Living Proof Air-Dry Styler, which contains hemisqualane for moisture that won’t weigh down fine strands. You can also experiment with a nourishing hair oil such as Moroccanoil’s Treatment, which is brimming with omega-6 for deep hydration.

In the evenings, Dr. Adel recommends wearing a silk or satin-lined scarf or bonnet to prevent friction and static as you sleep.

Replenish lost moisture with cocooning hair masks and treatments. Clark recommends incorporating keratin-based formulas to restore strength, while Clarke name-checks amino acids to increase hair’s hydrophobicity (this ultimately helps to lock in moisture), and hemisqualane to seal the cuticles so locks appear silkier.

Sam McKnight Hair Rich Nourish Conditioner

Ideally, try not to overstyle your hair with heated tools. “This can leave hair broken, dry, and even discolored,” says Clark. But, if you must use them (and most of us do prefer to), shield your strands with a heat protector, even if you’re just running a hair dryer through it. Look for one with hydrating, frizz-managing qualities to ease flyaways.

Wella Ultimate Smooth Miracle Hair Oil Serum

There’s a reason why some may find their grays looking lackluster. “Gray hair is more porous, meaning there is less natural protection from environmental factors (such as urban pollution) than with pigmented hair. This can be what causes a lack of shine or discoloration,” Clarke explains.

Modern shield formulas deliver hydration and protection against both heat tools and environmental damage.

Oribe Invisible Defense Universal Protection Spray

Beauty Works Solaré UV Leave-In Conditioning Mist

As a finishing touch, a small amount of hair oil will add extra shine to your grays, but a glossing treatment delivers luster that lasts. At-home glosses (which are often applied pre-conditioner or in place of it, left for a few minutes, then washed out) promise instant results. You can also use a semipermanent conditioning tint such as Shrine Drop It to revive the color of your grays.

#6723. Aryna Sabalenka, Coco Gauff, Mirra Andreeva, and More on Winning, Losing, Living, and Dreaming

Ahead of the season-ending WTA Finals tournament, kicking off Sunday at Indian Wells, the world’s eight highest-ranked women’s tennis players gathered for a fashion shoot and an easy hang. There, they talked exclusively to Vogue about their biggest wins, their toughest losses, their secret lives away from the court (pole dancing, UFC, baking cakes—who knew?)—and what they like to wear.

HEATED RIVALRY? Elina Svitolina, in Tom Ford, scores a snack while Rybakina, Gauff, and Muchova come away empty-handed.

The Indian Wells final was one of the best, because it was a really tough match, and I was a couple of match points down—I had to overcome a lot of things, and I got the win.

Obviously the Australian and US Open finals—in Australia [against Elena Rybakina], I had a break in the third set and felt like everything was going my way, but then it slipped, so I was really, really disappointed with that one. I should have won that one, but I didn’t. The US Open, not so much—[Rybakina] played really incredibly, and I didn’t.

When you walk out onto the court for a match, you’ve got headphones on. What are you listening to?

Sometimes nothing—sometimes I just like to block out the noise and stay in my thoughts. Sometimes I just put on some melodies that make me feel fired up. It’s always different—it just depends on my mood. I have a lot of favorite artists. I like Beyoncé. I like Rihanna. I like Dua Lipa, Tate McRae, Teddy Swims, Eminem, Justin Timberlake, 50 Cent, Britney Spears. I just need to rotate.

If you didn’t play any sport, what would you do for a career?

I think boxing or modeling—they’re so different, but both are things that I love.

Is there a sport other than tennis that you watch or play?

In Dubai—it’s actually crazy to say—but for the first time in my life I went to watch a UFC fight, and I became obsessed. I’m watching lots of fights now, and my entire algorithm is UFC and fighters. I became a huge fan of Khabib [Nurmagomedov, the undefeated UFC legend]. So, yeah, I’m crazy about UFC. I also like ice hockey, and I like to watch basketball and Formula One. I’d like to watch more MotoGP, but I cannot watch it because I’m like, How do you guys do that? It’s so dangerous. I feel so tight watching them race—I’m so scared for them.

I know that you like to get dressed up and that you’re no stranger to going big. You like a big heel, yeah?

Well, I love the way my body looks. But walking, as an athlete? It’s like a workout for me. I had to walk Vogue World in Milan, and I was just dying, because I’m not used to walking in high heels. But still, that was the best experience of my life.

Probably the US Open. I won the Australian Open at the beginning of the year, but the US Open just felt a little bit bigger this year, and New York is such a special city.

What’s your best weapon on the tennis court?

Just the aggressive style of my game. My serve can put me in a position where I can attack from the first ball and be dominant from the beginning of the point, and when that works, it doesn’t really matter who is on the other side.

When you’re away from the court, do you have a guilty pleasure, an indulgence, or a hobby?

I love sweets. With all the travel, I’m very sensitive, so it’s really not easy for me to just let it go and eat whatever I want, but yeah. When I get a chance, I kind of destroy myself—not just sweets, but everything baked: croissants, pain au chocolat.

HOLDING COURT From left: Karolina Muchova in Balenciaga. Sabalenka in a Nike jacket and Gucci skirt and shoes, Comme Si socks. Linda Noskova wears Missoni shorts and a jacket and white leather trench by The Frankie Shop; Miista boots. Pegula wears Chanel.

I played a really great match against Amanda [Anisimova] in Australia to make the semis, and then winning the Dubai title—being able to beat [Elina] Svitolina in the final—was really great. Everyone knows Dubai, and it’s cool to say, “Oh yeah, I won that title in Dubai.” I also played a really great match against Iva Jovic to make the quarterfinals in Wimbledon. I felt like I was able to go up two levels and kind of take the match from her, and to be able to do that against a younger player in a big situation felt great.

Did you have a hero or role model when you were growing up?

I didn’t watch a ton of tennis growing up—I was playing tennis—but my mom read me a lot of books about players, biographies and autobiographies, and I remember being drawn to Martina Hingis and Mary Pierce when my mom would read me their stories.

What’s your best weapon on the tennis court?

I’m very good at staying even-keeled and not wasting a lot of energy. It drains me when I’m wasting a lot of emotional energy. Some people play off of that and can handle it great, but I feel that gives me too many ups and downs.

One piece of advice for an average club player?

Sometimes I think people see pro players hit the ball and they’re like, Oh—I need to hit it harder. And you absolutely do not. I think that learning how to hit your medium rally ball that you can make 85% of the time is really important, because that’s something you can build your game around.

How do you get pumped up—or calmed down and focused—before a match?

I used to meditate quite a bit, and I feel like I can always go back to it if I’m feeling a nervous or anxious type of energy. Then I move on to just focusing on breathwork, which I think is so important for us when we’re on the court, too. Sometimes if you focus on your breath and let everything else just kind of happen, everything starts flowing and you get more instinctual, which I think is how you always want to play.

Do you have a guilty pleasure or something that you indulge yourself in when you’re away from tennis?

I play a lot of Call of Duty. Hours. I have a gaming laptop and I have a PS5 at home. One of my best friends and her boyfriend play, and my husband and I play with them all the time. I play with my brother and my sister a lot, too. I was a big Sims kid—sometimes I’ll whip that out and play for three days straight and then put it away for a year—and I went through a big Grand Theft Auto phase. I’ve heard mixed things about the new GTA—people are questioning the graphics—but let’s just say I’m interested.

If you didn’t play tennis—or any sport—what kind of job would you have?

When I was younger, I got really into hockey and always said that I wanted to be the first female GM of a hockey team. But now that I know too much, being a GM sounds really stressful.

When you’re getting dressed for a big night out, do you have a favorite piece, or something that you love that’s important to you?

I like traveling with a good dress and then elevating that with nice shoes or a purse or a jacket. And I’m definitely a jewelry person—that’s always been my thing.

You’re wearing Chanel here—were you a fan before this?

I got a really nice Chanel bag that I wore throughout my whole wedding weekend a few years ago, and I have a really nice pair of Chanel shoes, and another Chanel bag in a [Buffalo] Bills kind of blue that I’ve worn to games.

The Rome title—I had won there before twice, but winning there again as a mom, eight years later, was really a proud moment.

Did you have a hero or a role model growing up?

I really loved watching Andre Agassi—I loved his style of play and his presence on the court, and as a young player I always tried to imitate him, in a way: his spirit, his energy, the way he created the game on his own terms.

How do you get pumped up—or calmed down and focused—before a match?

Over the years, I’ve tried different tactics: Sometimes meditation works for me, sometimes it’s watching motivational videos, sometimes music—AC/DC, Eminem, Red Hot Chili Peppers. I also really love the spirit of Kobe Bryant and the way that he kind of went into this state.

Yeah, exactly—he was just really focused on the goal, the mission.

If you didn’t play any sport, what kind of job do you think you would have?

I would be a chef. Cooking really brings me joy, and when I’m home, I like to cook for the family. My grandmother and my mom are great cooks—I think it’s in our culture to prepare something nice.

CHEERING SECTION Clockwise, from top left: Pegula, Svitolina, Noskova, and Muchova are all gunning for number-one.

I mean, you don’t have to, but if I were you I probably would.

Yeah. From any perspective, that final was mentally and physically one of the toughest matches that I’ve ever played in my life.

How do you get pumped up—or calmed down and focused—before a match?

I usually like to calm down—I don’t really like to do anything right before my match, like listen to music or whatever, but a few hours before that I like to read: horror, something historical, a biography. I like a lot of different genres.

Do you have a guilty pleasure or something that you indulge yourself in when you’re away from tennis?

In my off-season, I like to travel to different places to see different cultures, different people, different languages. Last year I went to Zanzibar, in Tanzania, and volunteered at a local kindergarten for a week or 10 days, which was short but sweet, and I would love to go back there again.

Is there a sport other than tennis that you either watch or play?

I’ve been a huge fan of WWE since I was 14 or 15. It’s pretty weird for a European kid—I watched it on YouTube, but then when I was in America for the first time I put on some random channel and saw the wrestling and I was super pumped about it. That was my first time watching it live. I love Charlotte Flair, Sasha Banks, and some men as well, like the Undertaker and John Cena. Charlotte Flair was in my player’s box at the US Open this year—she’s obviously super strong and such an athlete, but at the same time, she’s a gorgeous woman, and so cool.

The finals in Doha—and playing doubles with Serena [Williams, in Berlin] was also so important, even if we lost in the first round. But it was a special match—just to have the chance to stand with such a champion as Serena and to practice with her.

What’s your best weapon on the tennis court?

My creativity—the way I can make the court very uncomfortable for my opponents…and for myself, sometimes, too.

How do you get pumped up—or calmed down and focused—before a match?

I listen to songs—different ones at every tournament. It can even be a slow song that brings you some feelings, but I always play that one song, and then I’m over it and go to another one. Lately it’s been just beats, fast songs, but it can be something from Beyoncé or Harry Styles, or some Czech pop songs.

Do you have a guilty pleasure or something that you indulge yourself in when you’re away from tennis?

I eat crazy food. I have a sweet tooth, so candy, chocolate, ice cream, pancakes; but I also like junk food, hamburgers, and everything that I can’t have when I play. I also play guitar—just to relax, as a hobby. I’ve been playing for about nine years, both acoustic and electric. I have a beautiful Takamine acoustic and a really nice Fender Stratocaster that my parents gave me for my birthday this year.

Is there a sport other than tennis that you watch or play?

My dad and my brother are both footballers—my dad is now a coach—so I watch Czech football, and when I’m in America I like to go watch the NBA or NHL.

When you’re getting dressed for a big night out, do you have a favorite piece, or something that you love that’s important to you?

I like to have a nice bag and jewelry, but overall I’m going for effortless and casual. I like simple pieces that look like I didn’t try too hard to put them together, even if I actually did.

SHINE ON Sabalenka, Gauff (wearing Tacori earrings and bracelets), Rybakina (wearing Tacori necklace and earrings) , and Mirra Andreeva (in Chanel) take to the stands instead of the court.

Probably the US Open quarterfinal against Mirra [Andreeva]—I saved two match points. I wasn’t really playing that well, but I fought really hard for that one. I also think the energy in New York just gives you an extra motivation to go the extra mile and never give up. And I’m always not giving up, but sometimes home court advantage is a thing.

Did you have a hero or a role model growing up?

The Williams sisters—Serena and Venus—are definitely my idols. Still are. Just seeing a woman of color dominating a sport that didn’t always cater to them historically. Also, their ability at merging sports, fashion, and culture is something that I always was interested in.

How do you get pumped up—or calmed down and focused—before a match?

Usually I try to meditate a little bit—I try to visualize myself just being successful in the match and seeing myself doing successful things. After that, honestly, I’m just on TikTok or just being normal.

Yes—usually some hype rap music, or sometimes some gospel—Kirk Franklin or Tye Tribbett. They don’t really sing; they’re more yelling and stuff, with a choir in the back that’s doing the singing for them. If you’ve ever been to a Black church, it’s kind of that style.

Paris—I just love it. It was the first city that I visited outside of the US, so I think I just always have nostalgia towards that, just realizing how far tennis could take me. It just feels like a home away from home a little bit. People always ask me for Paris recs, but I’m usually just the girl that will just go to the park by herself. I just like the vibe.

Do you have a guilty pleasure or something that you indulge yourself in when you’re away from tennis?

I just started like three weeks ago, but I really enjoy pole dancing. That’s been my thing. I’m one of those people that hobby jumps a lot—I bought a guitar and I haven’t used it; I bought a keyboard—so I need to stop wasting money on stuff that I’m interested in for two weeks. I’m hoping that this one sticks. It’s challenging though—I’m not very great, but one day.

Is there a sport other than tennis that you either watch or play?

I play basketball for fun—I’m not good, I just like it. And I watch American football and basketball—the Dolphins and the Heat—and then track and field when it’s the world championships and the Olympics.

When you’re getting dressed for a big night out, do you have a favorite piece, or something that you love that’s important to you?

I can probably count on my hands the amount of times I’ve went out—in my life—to a bar or club, but I do like to dress up. Sometimes I’ll dress up to just take pictures. Lately I’ve been loving a good heel, because I’m already tall and I just like being taller than people. But also a good bag. I just started working with Miu Miu, so I’ve been experimenting with outfits and stuff with them. They like to do a lot of layering, and layering was something I usually didn’t do because I’m from Florida and it’s hot, but it’s something that I’ve been trying to embrace more. And I love accessories, like a cute bow, or they have the bag charms now—anything to spice up your outfit.

Roland Garros—my first Grand Slam. The whole tournament was just something else. I still remember the emotions to this day. It was the very first tournament where I felt so focused—I could see every little hair on the tennis ball when I was about to hit the shot, and I haven’t ever experienced anything like that before.

Is there a loss this year that was important to you?

Yes—at the US Open when I lost, once again, to Coco Gauff. Coco is a very tough player that I don’t like playing against, but that’s okay. I had two match points—and obviously, with the New York crowd, I get that she would get 95% of the support, and I was actually dealing with that pretty good throughout the whole match. But having two match points to beat her for the first time and to advance to the semifinals of the US Open for the first time—there was a lot on the line that obviously didn’t go my way. That was very, very disappointing for me, and I was sad. But I think with time I’m able to learn from that.

Did you have a hero or a role model when you were growing up?

Yes, my role model was always Roger Federer. To this day I just adore him. For me, he is the best tennis player—not just the way he plays, but what kind of a person he is as well. I just love everything that he does.

I had a very, very quick chat with him at Wimbledon last year. He watched one of my matches and afterward he was there with a lot of other people and I just shook his hand, and he congratulated me and I just said that I’m a big, big fan. But it was very, very, very quick—maybe 20 seconds. But it’s better than nothing, so I’ll take it.

How do you get pumped up—or calmed down and focused—before a match?

I’ve actually been talking to my psychologist about this a lot. She told me that if I felt a little bit more calm before the match, maybe I wouldn’t be as nervous. So I have one routine where I listen to motivating, but calm, music—Billie Eilish, Lana Del Rey. Maybe I read a book for a bit. And then before every match, whether I’m calm or if I need a little bit more energy, I watch Roger Federer’s 2017 Australian Open final against Rafa Nadal—five sets, an amazing match. I don’t know how many times I’ve watched it, but I do it to feel the stress of the match, the adrenaline of how they both played. And when I need a little bit more energy, I play Uno with my team. That’s where things get serious—that’s where we can fight a little bit. I also listen to more energetic music—Bon Jovi, Queen. A little bit of older times, but that’s my taste in music.

If you didn’t play any sport, what kind of job would you have?

I’ve been thinking about this a lot recently. For sure I would study more, go to university—but I also think maybe I might want to try acting. I don’t know—my mom says that I’m a pretty good actor when, like, something happens and I need to make it look like I don’t know what’s going on. Maybe I would just give it a shot and see how I would do.

You don’t seem like a stranger to getting dressed up and going out with your friends—

I love to dress up, and maybe a half a year ago I was manifesting heels, because I had never owned high heels in my life. I was talking about high heels everywhere, in every interview, and then I got a high heel from my agent as a gift. But since then, they’ve just been coming at me. Now I have 10 pairs. I don’t wear a super high heel because otherwise I’d break my leg, but I love to put little heels with everything I wear—with jeans, with pants, with a skirt. I think they make the outfit look a little more elegant, and now, for some reason I like the elegant lifestyle.
