#6721. From Caramelized Amber to Bombshell Blowouts, These Are Fall’s Biggest Hair Trends

Every item on this page was chosen by an ELLE editor. We may earn commission on some of the items you choose to buy.

Hairstylists share the buzziest fall hair trends their clients can’t get enough of.

When dried leaves in varying hues of orange, red, and yellow crunch under our feet, it’s basically a bat signal that the best season is underway. Fall sits right in the middle of summer’s balmy rays and winter’s biting chill, with a refreshing briskness that won’t necessarily expedite reversion for curly hair going straight and won’t dry out freshly bleached and/or dyed strands. The options are endless in this kind of weather, which can make decision-making feel a bit overwhelming. Do you try a new color? A bob cut? Maybe a pixie? According to the hottest hair trends of the season, you can do it all.

The transition from summer to fall is an important one for your hair. “Hair can be a little more compromised or porous based on the environment, from swimming pools and sun in the summer. Going from fall to winter, hair treatments to encourage hydration and strength are the easiest way to get your hair back on track,” says Eric Marshall Wright, stylist and owner of Eric Marshall Salon in Nashville, Tennessee. With a proper hair routine at home, your hair becomes strong enough to withstand your next hair transformation—that’s where fall’s biggest hair trends come in.

If you’re itching for a new hairdo, we polled several hairstylists, including Wright, to see what they predict will be the most head-turning hairstyles of the season, straight from their very own salons. Whether you’re a balayage connoisseur or tempted to do a bob, allow this list of trends to inspire you ahead of your next appointment.

Here’s a subtle take on the popular balayage technique that works with your hair color, creating a soft gradient with lowlights and highlights. “These highlights are soft, tone-on-tone highlights with dimension—think of them as a soft whisper in an overstimulated world. They look underdone instead of overdone; it’s a delicate hair color that’s sustainable and grounded. The look is effortlessly cool, glossy, and glazed for a finish that’s organically imperfect,” says Leslie Shores, color specialist at Eric Marshall Salon. This shade is perfect for “anyone who prefers a timeless, sustainable color. It’s achieved with no bleach, lightener, balayage, or ammonia-free demi-permanent hair color. Ask your colorist for soft tone-on-tone color.”

Sometimes the road to blonde is far too intimidating from dark brown or black. Shores’ answer to that gives you a lift without veering too much into blonde territory. “Cocoa brondette,” she says, is “a rich brunette with soft ribbons of deep indulgent brown shades.” The color is reminiscent of a rich cup of hot cocoa, with swirls of light brown throughout. “This shade looks best on someone with an olive skin tone, and can be achieved with demi-permanent or permanent hair color or with balayage. Ask your colorist for an all-over color with ammonia-free color around a level seven, six, or five; they can also paint soft ribbons of balayage.”

While most of the world is obsessed with bobs and pixies, another percentage of the population still favors long locks. Dimitris Giannetos, celebrity hairstylist and Great Lengths ambassador, says long hair isn’t going anywhere. “Hair can take a long minute to grow, so I have the help of Great Lengths, especially the Linea Wefts, to achieve the perfect, lived-in long hair,” he shares. His favorite hair trend this season? “CEO blowout,” which looks polished “but secure enough to get a bit messy.” This looks even better when paired with a “quiet, lived-in color, with more wispy, secret highlights versus an obvious balayage,” he adds. Your tools to achieve this are simple: “I use three different shades of the Great Lengths Line Wefts. They have such a fine spine, which makes them easy to blend and fully match your client’s color with an extra twist. They are super flat on the scalp, so they blend together perfectly without unwanted volume on the sides. I always recommend razoring the wefts at the end to create the perfect blend,” Giannetos says.

Wright concurs, adding that layers can elevate long styles that “looks effortless and moves.” Placement matters when it comes to layering hair, depending on the style you wear most often. “Layers can be as short as collarbone so you can easily put it up, but this is more about wearing it down and long-styled. Think hippie boho or 60s and long like Pocahontas. The cut is accomplished by point cutting and dry cutting techniques to make it soft and lived-in, not overly aggressive but effortless layers,” Wright shares.

If you want a louder balayage, Shores encourages you to opt for “rich shades of buttery gold and copper throughout the hair that look warm, rich, cozy, and earthy.” The gradient of hues might immediately scream summer, but it offers a toasted finish that “adds exotic warmth, depth, and dimension to the hair that feels like golden hour. Ask your colorist to paint big balayage pieces mainly in the front of the hair to match the volume and layers. These can be foiled or painted on. It looks best on brunettes and someone with thicker hair with layers.”

Already blonde? Shores suggests “bright, airy white-blonde balayage highlights that are airy and dreamy placed perfectly, as they carry a lightness to them that make them look ethereal and serene.” This look works great for those who are already “bright platinum without the constant touch up. [It’s also] perfect also for grey blending. This look can be achieved by using bleach balayage or foilyage. Ask your colorist to use bleach balayage or foilyage to get as light as possible!” she adds.

“Thanks to Off Campus and [actress] Ella Bright, we’re gravitating towards this shoulder-length bob that is worn flipped, sleek, curled, or blown out,” Wright says. Pictured here, this bob is marked by an asymmetrical blunt cut and soft waves throughout. “The cut needs to have facial shape and neck width taken into consideration, as those will cause different results, as well as the natural density and hair diameter,” Wright adds.

With summer’s sticky weather behind us, fall’s coolness means those bangs you’ve been dying to get won’t get too stuck to your forehead. “Being in a humid environment, they can devastate you in the summer, as the humidity makes them fussy. A fringe or bang can make you look styled and undone at the same time, meaning you can just style your bangs and pull your hair up to look chic. I recommend a fuller style rather than wispy so they look intentional. Keep hairline, cowlicks, and recession in mind, as bangs can have a mind of their own; style them first, as they can be difficult to dry on their own. For a softer, fuller look, ask your stylist to point-cut the ends for softness,” Wright explains.

Davines This is a Dry Texturizing Finishing Spray

“For long, high-volume natural textures, go with Davines Dry Texturize. This enhances volume on the mid-shaft through ends, especially for those who like texture and volume on their ends. Clipping [the hair] back [is an easy way] to give high volume to a half-up/half-down look and secure it with a claw clip.”—Eric Marshall Wright

“Those with sleek or textured bobs, I personally would recommend the Davines Shimmering Mist, as it creates high shine with zero hold. This could really emphasize the texture of the bob whether it’s straight or blown out or done with waves.”—EMW

Davines Hair Refresher, Dry Cleansing Shampoo

“As far as bangs go, I highly recommend the Davines Hair Refresher because bangs can be tricky and you sometimes need to rewash them. It’s nice to have something that is powder base to refresh them, that way you’re not re-styling them or rewetting them—you’re just refreshing them.”—EMW

Featuring a fall-ready leopard design, Wright loves these clips for tightly securing long hair in half-up, half-down styles.

#6719. Crying in the Club (and Everywhere Else) With Jordan Firstman

“This is what you’re keeping me from right now,” Jordan Firstman says, and pivots his laptop screen to face a high hotel window overlooking a long, tempting stretch of Brazilian beach.

Firstman is in Rio de Janeiro for work, presenting three film-festival screenings of Club Kid, his directorial debut, which he also wrote and stars in as Peter, a dissolute downtown New York club promoter whose own extended adolescence ends abruptly when he’s called upon to parent Arlo, the 10-year-old son he’s never met.

The Brazilian audiences “really got it,” Firstman reports. It seems like everybody who watches Club Kid really gets it. The film received a seven-minute ovation at the Cannes Film Festival back in May, and sold to A24 for a reported $17 million after a brief, buzz-stoking bidding war. Preview screenings in LA, where Firstman lives, have been packed to the rafters.

Shirt and pants by Brioni. Bow tie and cummerbund, stylist’s own. Vintage watch by Rolex from Foundwell. Vintage cufflinks by Cartier from Foundwell. Earring, his own.

But when it’s suggested that this all bodes well for Club Kid’s broader appeal when it finally hits theaters, Firstman says, “Only time will tell. I hope it translates to the gen-pop.”

What we do know: Club Kid is hands down the most heartwarming film ever made about a man raising a child conceived during a blotto bisexual threesome—a supremely confident comedy-drama, raw and honest about gay sex, party drugs, and parenting in a way that’s excitingly and delightfully at odds with the sweetness of its tone. It’s an extremely likeable film, and its director-star is extremely likeable in it. And, I’ll say—at the risk of being rude—this means it’s kind of a departure for Firstman, who up until now has cultivated an almost proudly polarizing comedic persona online and onscreen. “I think, when you’re annoying and gay, people can’t get past that, in our culture,” he says, “and it’s interesting to me.”

Firstman is 35, and has not been famous particularly long, but if his public life so far has taught him anything, it’s how quickly the wind can shift. He broke through doing silly front-facing video sketches during COVID—playing banana bread’s publicist, yass-ing up his new favorite client, that sort of thing—and before long found himself apologizing for unearthed edgelord tweets he’d written in his early 20s. (He said in a statement that he’d “grown a million lifetimes” since those posts.)

His run on Fox’s English Teacher ended with the show’s cancellation in 2025; around the same time, he popped off to Vulture about the sex scenes in Heated Rivalry, suggesting the hockey bromance didn’t have a clue about “how gay people fuck.” (He is perhaps the only person ever to have pissed off that show’s fan base and lived to tell the tale, which may be evidence that nothing can stop his rise.)

Now ensconced once again as a TV-series regular—on HBO’s I Love LA—and with a buzzy movie in the pipeline, he’s able to look at all this with sunrise/sunset serenity.

“There’s ebbs and flows to whether people fuck with you or not,” he says. “Everyone loved me during the pandemic, and then everyone hated me for a little bit, and now it feels like people like me again.”

Still, he remains, by his own admission, “too online,” unable to not read things written about him, and it’s hard not to internalize some of that stuff, a little bit. He was gay and annoying in 2023’s Rotting in the Sun, playing “Jordan Firstman,” a dick-swinging, clout-chasing imp who torments a depressive artist played by the film’s director, Sebastián Silva. No less an authority than Pedro Almodóvar saw the movie and told Firstman he was a “real actor,” but his was one of the kinder reactions.

“I kind of assumed audiences would understand it was a performance,” Firstman says, “and I think many didn’t.” He thinks the movie is brilliant and calls Silva a genius. But he’s also convinced that playing a maximally annoying caricature of himself “really did affect the way people saw me, and then it affected how I saw myself. The year after Rotting was actually very tough for me, because I felt very hated.”

The new film, he says, is partly a response to that experience, he says. “I think Club Kid came from a place of, ‘I know how I feel, and I know how I’m being perceived is so different than how I feel, and I want to show a more true side of myself through this work.’”

That wasn’t how it started, of course. It started with Firstman at a dinner party, doing bits with his friends’ kid. That was the spark—Firstman realizing that putting a Jordan Firstman–type character, talking the way he does, in situations with an impressionable minor who maybe shouldn’t hear the kinds of things Firstman tends to say out loud, could be a great comedic setup.

Club Kid is in conversation with a long line of films about characters thrust into a parental role they’re ill-equipped for; Firstman can rattle them off, from Chaplin’s The Kid to Auntie Mame to Kramer vs. Kramer to Big Daddy. But as he wrote, bigger ideas emerged—about the “arrested development” of a certain cohort of childless gay men, about what it actually means to be an adult. And in working out how Peter would show up to his newfound relationship with Arlo, he thought about his own parents—two Newsday reporters who raised him in the New York suburbs—and what he got from them, as well as what he wished he’d gotten.

“I feel like no one taught me what life was going to be like. We just got by in a pleasant-ish way. But I don’t think I got major insights,” he says. A beat. “It is what it is. I am grateful that I went looking for those insights in my early 20s, through drug trips.”

This is what it’s like to talk to Firstman these days; he’s reflective, but he’ll still spring a provocative overshare on you like a trap door. (Boing! Drug trips!) The first time we met, at a photo shoot a few weeks before the call from Brazil, he told me that although the standing ovation thing at Cannes is overblown (“It felt great, but it’s such a ruse. It’s like, you can keep it going if you want. You just don’t let it stop. [From the stage] You keep pointing at different people in the movie”), the experience of showing the movie to an appreciative audience at the most prestigious film festival in the world had been transformative, that it felt like “20 years of validation that I didn’t get,” and that he no longer feels the same need to “say the edgy thing” all the time.

But at the very beginning of that conversation—as I remember it, we were still in the process of shaking hands—he started telling me an off-the-record story involving, let’s say, an adult situation. Today, over Zoom, I ask if that anecdote (explicit, slightly alarming) was the old Jordan briefly reasserting himself by saying the edgy thing.

“It probably came from a place of, maybe, nervousness, if I’m being honest,” he says. “But I think, probably, there was some sort of provocation that was a bit of a shield in that story.”

And it’s more complicated than that, he notes—because the guy who says the edgy thing is a part of him, too, and who’s to say it’s not his best self? He really does feel, after Cannes, like he doesn’t have to prove himself in quite the same way, he says.

“But then I’m like, ‘Oh, am I changing into something that’s less honest, or more honest? Are the gritty parts of me honest, and I’m letting go of them to be more palatable?’” Or is it a defense mechanism, “and the real me is something softer and sweeter and more put-together?”

The goal, of course, is to amalgamate all our disparate selves. Wouldn’t that be great? Firstman has tried his best.

“I’ve done a lot,” he says. “Everything mystical, I’ve tried.”

He’s tried past-life regression, and he’s tried ayahuasca, and he’s the second person I’ve interviewed—the first being Mike Tyson—who has tried bufotenin, a hallucinogen found in the venom of the Sonoran desert toad. (He doesn’t recall much about the first time he tried it, except a feeling “like something really bad happened”; the second time was “a way more positive, beautiful experience.”)

“I think I’ve always been a very curious person,” he says. “They say with ayahuasca, it finds you when you’re supposed to do it.”

When he heard about ayahuasca—a traditional psychoactive tea brewed from two plants native to the Amazon—on comedian Duncan Trussell’s podcast, he says, “It felt like I got shot in the stomach. I was like, ‘I have to do this.’” The next day he was at a party and somebody told him they’d just done it, under the supervision of a shaman in Topanga. Firstman went on to do it nine times over the course of his 20s.

“By the end, it kicked me out,” he says. “God, literally, was like, ‘You can’t come back here. This realm is not for you, ever again.’ I still did it one more time after that, and it was like, Bitch, are you serious? It almost really fucked me up.”

So he was pushing it, he reasons, with the toad venom. “I maybe shouldn’t have even done that, but I think it’s a different thing.”

He has this secret spiritual tool kit now, of stuff he’s learned from these experiences, about his own perceptions, and he thinks it’s protected him. He wasn’t looking for a way out of anything or relief from any particular suffering or struggle. He wanted to learn about life and what there was to experience—which, as it happens, is also how he’s approached his working life.

“I do it through film, I do it through music. I do it through social interactions. I think life is about learning in any way you can and experiencing everything you can.”

Instagram videos. Sitcoms. Directing a movie. Each another trip: What happens when I do this? He figures he could probably have built a more stable career, “if I had a more diligent respect for one medium, maybe.” But he can’t help where his creative impulses take him. Was anybody clamoring for Firstman to make 2025’s Secrets, a full-length comedy album of oddly well-executed genre-parody songs with titles like “I’m Hoarding Cum” and “Pennies in My Pussy”?

The answer is no. (The actual answer is probably “not at all.”) But once he started making the record, Firstman says, “there was no stopping me. I was in the studio, like, ‘What am I doing in a music studio?’ But I couldn’t not. I was there every day. I was begging any producer I knew to help me, because I just needed to.”

Chances are you could not make a movie like Club Kid, whose realness stems in part from a clearly lived-in understanding of partying, without having done some wild shit. But it would be difficult to make this movie if you were still living that way. Peter has Arlo to drop-kick him out of suspended adolescence and into adulthood; I ask Firstman what the catalyst was for his own growth.

“I think it was a slow process,” he says, “that’s still happening, to some degree.”

Some of what happened was professional: In 2025, he put out the album and shot the second season of English Teacher, the first season of I Love LA, and Club Kid. The practical demands of that schedule forced him to lock in: “I didn’t have Saturdays off to party, and I couldn’t afford, on a Monday, to not feel like my best.”

He also went through a breakup “that was really, really, really sad and just really unexpected, and someone I never thought I would break up with.”

He doesn’t want to be too specific about, y’know, the specifics. But it was a split he initiated.

“It came to a point where I was like, ‘I know the life I want to live and I don’t think this love is aligning with that life.’ I had to choose my life over love—which is such a mind-fuck, because you’re like, ‘Love is everything. There’s nothing more important than love.’ But then, your life is also—on a day-to-day level, it’s pretty important. And so yeah, I think it was a really tough, bizarre out-of-body experience almost, because it was a love I had never known the likes of before, and then it was over.”

By the time they broke up they had been together for four years. When it started, Firstman says, he couldn’t believe they’d found each other and the depth of what he was feeling for this person. “And I felt the exact same way with the breakup,” he says. “I was like, ‘I cannot believe this is happening.’ It feels so unreal. It just doesn’t make any sense. As much as the love didn’t make sense in the beginning, how powerful it felt, the breakup didn’t. It was the exact same feeling.

After their last conversation they agreed to stay friends, and then they didn’t talk for a year. “I think he was protecting himself and maybe protecting me too,” Firstman says. When his ex finally responded to a message, Firstman was on set, about to shoot a climactic scene in Club Kid—he’d scripted, as it happens, a big emotional moment for Peter, a moment where two characters connect on the phone after a long time apart.

“The first time, in a year, he had responded, was the moment before they called ‘Action,’” Firstman says. “That’s why I cried so hard in that scene, just like a huge release.”

His ex hasn’t seen the movie yet, Firstman says, and maybe he never will. It’s dedicated to him, though—his name is in the end credits. “He doesn’t know that either,” he says. “I’m a little scared. I’m a little scared, because to me, the movie is a love letter to him.”

He starts crying here, a little bit, apologizing even as it’s happening.

“All of that extra love that I still have for him, I put it directly into the movie. If he does see it, which I don’t expect him to or need him to, I hope he sees that’s where all my love went, and that I still have it for him and I always will.”

He has not started writing his next movie yet, but he’s started thinking about it. He knows that like this one, it’ll be a love story—and that after writing, in Club Kid, about familial love, community love, and loving yourself, he wants to write about friendship next.

In the past year, he’s been blown away by two movies of vast scope, Paul Thomas Anderson’s One Battle After Another (“I was making my movie when that came out, and I think that is a movie, for him, about growing up, and not feeling like a grown-up as an adult”) and the equally sprawling queer epic La Bola Negra. I ask him if he’s looking to go similarly big with his next project. Maybe, he says.

“But I think I’d like to take incremental steps and learn more as a filmmaker before.…”

“Yeah,” he says, laughing. “My war movie. The Firstman war movie. I have zero context for war, so I would be completely making everything up.” ✦

#6714. Kevin Costner Is Particular About Scents—So He Made His Own Colognes

Eight years ago, Kevin Costner was in Germany on a press tour. His hotel room was chock full of fruit baskets and other fancy accouterments that come with international fame. And also a handful of bath products. “I’m taking a shower and I’m thinking, ‘Man, this body wash smells good,’” he tells me from the couch of his modern white compound on a seaside street in Carpinteria, California. “And I’m thinking, ‘I don’t really use those words. Why would I even think that to myself?” Maybe two more times on that 15-day junket, he found himself thinking about the scent of that body wash.

“Can’t tell you why, don’t even know what it was,” he says. “I came back home to America, and probably over the next year, periodically, I actually thought about it. But then it faded in like a song you can’t remember.”

A few years later, he found himself in Scotland, scoring his Western epic Horizon. After a jetlagged detour to a countryside castle, he hopped in a hotel shower in Glasgow, and there it was: the smell. “I looked down and there were the bottles and I go, ‘That’s that smell from five or six years ago. That’s that smell,’" he recounts with his English lab, Bob, curled up at his side. “And I did something incredibly stupid. I went out of the shower and I got my phone.”

He got water everywhere in the process, but at that moment he was singularly focused. “I go back in the shower and I take a picture of these bottles as if they were going to disappear. I could have just really finished my shower, honestly. Dried off like a normal human being. But what I’m saying was it fired my senses again, imagination. And I sent those pictures back and I said, ‘See if you can get a case of this. I’m never going to forget it again.’”

It turned out to be 19-69’s Rainbow Bar, a scent inspired by both the ‘80s glam rock bands that frequented the Rainbow Bar on the Sunset Strip, along with general notes of California: there’s bourbon alongside basil and vetiver, creating a fragrance that’s simultaneously woody and green. That kickstarted Costner’s career as a perfumer. Now, he’s debuting a collection of fragrances with the same Milan-based niche perfume house. The collection consists of three fragrances (or extrait de parfum, to be precise), chicly advertised on 19-69’s website with a photo of Kevin Costner’s star on the Hollywood Walk of Fame. They retail at $80 per 7.5 milliliter bottle (a 30 ML bottle will run you $300, and the really giant 95 ML version costs a cool $800), and each fragrance—called After Hours, Heritage, and Pacific Coast Highway—reflects something of Costner’s life and history.

Kevin Costner first discovered 19-69 after using its body wash during a press tour in Germany, but it wasn't until years later he figured out the brand's name.

He tells me this story from his living room, amid coffee table books on design and the American frontier, and a homemade scrapbook dedicated to Bob’s first year of life (the dog peed a little bit on my foot, but I took it as a compliment). I visited on a foggy day in June, walking into his home to be greeted by a view of the Pacific. Costner, who has an endless string of massive, monocultural hits—Field of Dreams, The Bodyguard, the tv show Yellowstone—has the aura of a Paul Newman-type, his bright blue eyes undiminished by the trail of drool and dog hair that Bob left on his feather-light black sweater. The peculiarity that we are talking about his collaboration with 19-69, and not an upcoming film of his, is not lost on him. “I bring just a lot of feeling to things because I can’t always explain why I like something,” he says. “It’s like wine. I think, ‘oh, it smells like wood.’ But does it, really? The fuck it does.”

After his second encounter with 19-69 products in Scotland, Costner’s assistant eventually tracked the brand’s co-founder Johan Bergelin down, and 19-69 sent him a case of the product. In 2024, he called Bergelin, to congratulate him on a job well done. They met in person for the first time that August in Cologne, Germany, which was not on purpose but did make them laugh. Shortly after that first meeting, they went ahead with a partnership, spending two years developing a collection of fragrances, produced in France.

As a child growing up in a small town in the Skåne region of Sweden, Bergelin had, much like Costner, been seduced by a scent he encountered in the wild. His was a perfume at the local hair salon, a mass market scent from Karl Lagerfeld. An artist and designer, he eventually became a self-taught perfumer, and launched 19-69 in 2017 with his wife, Catharina, who handles communications and writes the colorful copy for each scent. The Milan-based brand—initially inspired by the culture and societal upheaval of 1969, the year of Bergelin’s birth—is known amongst self-described “fragheads” for its offerings tied to specific eras and places (Christopher Street, the Rainbow Bar in Hollywood, the island of Capri): their Miami Blue scent has a note of cocaine; the American Psycho perfume, a collaboration with Bret Easton Ellis (which just won an Allure “Best of Beauty” award), contains hints of palate-cleansing sorbet and harkens back to the products in Patrick Bateman’s prophetic 1980s beauty routine; Female Christ references a 1969 performance piece by Danish artist Lene Adler Petersen, in which she walked naked through the Copenhagen Stock Exchange carrying a cross. For the Costner collection, they’ve developed a group of three scents, titled After Hours, Pacific Coast Highway, and Heritage, all based on the actor’s life.

After Hours, the signature scent of the collection, has notes of cypress, bourbon, and nutmeg; Bergelin describes as a version of 19-69’s Rainbow Bar fragrance “on steroids,” and says that for him, it evokes the image of someone in a glass house in the Hollywood Hills at sunset, surveying the city. It reminds Costner of shooting one of his first major magazine covers, the May 1989 issue of Vanity Fair, with the louche, legendary Helmut Newton. “So, I was in a tuxedo but my tie was off and my jacket was on the couch,” he recounts. “It was supposed to be a sexy shot with a glass of whiskey. And Helmut kept saying, ‘take your shirt off, just leave the bow tie on or something’... I said no. I’m not an exotic dancer!” He carefully notes that Newton was “so sweet” and did not make this suggestion in any sort of predatory fashion. He was merely opposed to looking like a Chippendale.

Costner (left) first met 19-69 co-founder Johan Bergelin (right) in 2024 and together they spent two years developing a trio of fragrances inspired by the actor's life.

Costner once wore After Hours to one of his son’s volleyball tournaments. “There were about 15 teams of teenage boys,” he says. “So the gym smelled really bad.” He says a pregnant woman kept staring at him, with her friend tugging her arm, urging her not to approach. “She walks all across the gym towards me,” he says. “And I wasn’t sure what this was going to be about. And she just turns to me and says, ‘Look, I’m married, I’m not [trying to bother you]. But what are you wearing?’” She did not ask for an autograph.

“The scent doesn’t have to be obvious,” he says. “But I love that it somehow becomes noticeable on its own merit, period.”

Pacific Coast Highway is lighter, with notes of clementine, juniper berry, and jasmine, Bergelin’s favorite. It smells like going to the beach in California (on a day without an algae bloom or whatever) and then taking a long hot shower after. It is clean without being boring, and I love it. Costner says the PCH scent reminds him of Tommy James and the Shandell’s 1968 hit “Crystal Blue Persuasion,” a lysergic earworm inspired by the Books of Isaiah, Ezekiel, and Revelations that most listeners and critics instead took to be a song about acid, amphetamines, or meth. “It’s easy,” he says. “A light sensory moment.”

Heritage is a rich, masculine scent that nods to life on Costner’s sprawling ranch in Aspen, Colorado, with notes of cherry, violet leaves, amber, and vanilla, scents that sound sweet and girly on paper but add up to something whiskey-ish (“It’s on the richer side,” says Bergelin. “It has volume.”) Costner says it reminds him of “a place that’s very masculine, carpets and wood and guns and there’s a deepness to it like the wood of a place. It has a forest-y feeling to me.”

Costner, an avid hunter, is eager to talk about guns as we sniff Heritage. He both believes in laws that limit them and sees them as heirlooms, like jewelry. “If you misuse a gun, you should never have one again,” he says. “But I have my father’s gun, and he got it when he was young. And so, when I put that gun to my cheek, I can feel him. When I was a boy, I would just ask him to let me hold it and it was much too heavy for me. And now it feels almost light as a feather. And my sons will one day put the gun to their cheek when I won’t be here, and they’ll remember those times in the field with that dog and everything else.”

19-69’s tagline is “bottling counterculture.” But Costner, born in 1955, had a different experience of the hippie years. He was raised in a conservative household without much money in Southern California; his late brother left to serve in the Marines in Vietnam while other kids his age protested the war. He rigorously studied classical piano with an elderly instructor who had been around long enough to teach FDR. “You can imagine where the politics were with my mother and father, who wanted to support their son in Vietnam,” he says. “At the dinner table, long hair was bad. The music was bad. They didn’t like anything about it. And I was sitting there eating at that same table thinking I liked a lot of it.”

He was too young to go full Woodstock. But he remembers what it was like to be around the culture. “A whole generation here went north to the Haight-Ashbury, to San Francisco, the Summer of Love,” he remembers. “I would watch the last exit out of Santa Barbara when there was no freeway. It was just a highway with lights, and the last one was like a last man out of Saigon moment. There would sometimes be as many as 60, 70 kids at that light with their thumbs out.”

Costner’s best-known roles are visceral and sexy, and in watching them, it’s easy to conjure up scents: saddle leather, the grass of the Great Plains and baseball parks, sweat, campfires, gunpowder. Millions of people have formed their own relationships with him by going to the movies, surrounded by the scents of melted butter and spilled soda. One 2016 study examined the olfactory experience of going to the cinema, in which chemists asserted that audiences emitted different compounds, like carbon dioxide and isoprene, depending on the genre of film they were watching, unwittingly creating new scents for emotional or romantic scenes. If that’s true, which seems awfully nice to believe, Costner has, in one small way, been in the fragrance business for a long time.

He says his favorite smells are lemon, cinnamon, and sage (“I knew [sage] as a hunter, not as an in-crowd thing”), and his house smells like cleanliness, or nothing. I asked if he likes the smell of movie theaters. “Not particularly,” he says. “I think what I miss in a theater is the curtain. But I know that smell of popcorn. It’s almost ceremonial, in a way, and it’s always lousy. It’s better when you cook it at home, it just is.”

#6713. Kate Middleton Goes Cozy Mode to Visit a Charity Close to Her Heart

Kate Middleton was serendipitously on-theme for the 2027 Met Gala for a recent visit to Dose of Nature, a UK-based mental health charity. On November 6, the Prince and Princess of Wales shared glimpses on Instagram from Princess Catherine’s visit, which reportedly took place in late October.

“A wonderful visit to pioneering mental health charity Dose of Nature, which supports people experiencing mental health challenges through a clinically led program that combines psychology, connection with nature and one-to-one guidance,” the post’s caption says. Along with photos of the Princess smiling as she looks on at people watercoloring outdoors, the post shared a video of a conversation with the charity’s founders, Dr. Alison Greenwood and Dr. Georgina Gould, who discussed how time in nature helps people feel calmer.

For the visit, the princess layered up in what looked to be a Barbour jacket (from Alexa Chung’s collection) paired with a navy blue turtleneck sweater and & Other Stories blue jeans. Of course, Kate Middleton is no stranger to some heritage chic, often reaching for a Burberry trench or a barn jacket for a mosey around the outdoors.

The power of nature holds great personal meaning for the Princess, who has spoken about how nature helped her heal during her cancer recovery. She has been in remission since January 2025, and for her 44th birthday in January 2026, she shared a poignant final installment of “Mother Nature,” her video series that explored the relationship between nature, mental health, and healing.

#6712. ELLE Escapes: Palm Beach

Every item on this page was chosen by an ELLE editor. We may earn commission on some of the items you choose to buy.

There’s just something about Palm Beach. Maybe it’s the namesake trees, the prime people-watching, or the air of exclusivity that comes with its private beaches and members-only clubs. Whatever the draw, this laid-back island feels more desirable than ever, even if a presidential visit to Mar-a-Lago means contending with a little extra gridlock. Roll down the windows, leave reality behind, and settle into one of Florida’s most rarefied corners for a weekend of luxury, indulgence, and enviable living. Ahead, I’ve rounded up where the well-heeled snowbirds eat, drink, and shop on their next trip down south.

With shops like Zimmermann, Hermès, and Veronica Beard, a tempting lineup of restaurants, and even a gelato stand at Sant Ambreous, the John Volk-designed Royal Poinciana Plaza is more than enough to fill an afternoon, and you’ll be happy to let it.

Golf and Palm Beach go hand in hand. If you’re a novice like me, this scenic par-3 course overlooking the water is the ideal place to work on your swing—or relive those regrettable bogeys long after you’ve left the green.

Step into the spa at Eau Resort & Spa, and it’s immediately clear why it earned a place in the hotel’s name. From the impeccable service and indulgent treatments to the top-tier facilities, the sprawling 42,000-square-foot space is the ultimate place for a little (or a lot of) pampering.

Lack of Color Utopia Inca Raffia Bucket Hat

Does it get any better than Nobu? From its signature miso black cod and rock shrimp tempura to the yellowtail jalapeño and specialty rolls, every dish is a standout. Add impeccable presentation to the mix, and this Japanese-Peruvian favorite never disappoints. Its new location at the Eau is no exception.

Set on the picturesque terrace of The Brazilian Court Hotel, this much-talked-about Daniel Boulud-helmed restaurant lives up to the hype. You really can’t go wrong with anything on the menu, but the White Cosmo (a mix of vodka, elderflower, and white cranberry, finished with an orchid ice cube) is begging to be Instagrammed.

For the uninitiated, the Nora (North of the Railroad) District in West Palm Beach is quickly becoming the city’s next big thing, and Del Mar is helping lead the charge. Steps away from the newly opened Nora Hotel, its Mediterranean-inspired menu and sprawling 12,000-square-foot space, complete with a 100-seat courtyard, feel both inviting and refined. Don’t miss the Open Fire Roasted Shellfish Tower, made for sharing (though I won’t judge if you keep it all to yourself).

Farm Rio Golden Yellow Anthurium Square Neck Mini Dress

Alexis Bittar Liquid Lucite Front Back Hoop Earring

Andrea Gomez Bella Raffia Platform Sandals

Open for breakfast, lunch, or dinner, Swifty’s, the poolside restaurant at The Colony Hotel, proves that casual dining can still deliver. Stick around for the live music, particularly the acoustic guitarists who stick to the hits (no requests necessary). And before you call it a day, make a pit-stop at the pool-deck newsstand to pick up the latest issue of ELLE.

HMF, the restaurant and lounge at The Breakers, is a great spot for a pre-dinner drink before wandering the resort’s storied halls. And its wine credentials are nothing short of legendary: It’s earned a Grand Award from Wine Spectator every year since the awards program began in 1981.

Just a block from the ocean, this picturesque, pink-hued property packs plenty into its 79 rooms, including a sunset-facing pool deck, a gym, a ballroom, and, of course, a stunning bar.

Coniglio Palm Beach Cinch Back Silk Midi Skirt

Tucked away on Lake Mangonia in West Palm Beach, the Belgrove Resort & Spa has all the makings of a perfect getaway. Think an 18-hole golf course, four tennis courts, two pickleball courts, two padel courts, private balconies in every guest room, a gym, a spa, three pools, and two hot tubs. Whether you’re after an action-packed escape or some serious R&R, you’ll find it here. And when you’re ready to venture out, a complimentary shuttle will take you anywhere within a five-mile radius.

Sizable suites? Check. A private, shaded pool and on-site hair salon? Check. Custom Linus bikes to borrow and complimentary yacht rides? Absolutely. The Brazilian Court Hotel feels like a true home base in the heart of town, just a quick ride from the Palm Beach Lake Trail. As owner Courtney Schlesinger puts it: “The hotel was built to feel like a private estate, so when you’re here, you feel like you have your own place in Palm Beach. That’s what I love the most: waking up in the morning, sitting on the terrace with a coffee, and imagining Daniel Boulud is my own private chef.”

A little off the beaten path and about a 20-minute drive from Palm Beach, Eau Resort & Spa more than makes up for its location with direct beach access, guest rooms designed by Jonathan Adler, two pools, a world-class spa, and a full-service beauty salon offering manicures, pedicures, and blowouts. Add six restaurants (including Nobu) and kid-friendly perks like childcare and an arcade, and you have everything you need for a getaway without ever leaving the property. So why would you?

#6710. What It’s Really Like Being the Third in a Threesome

“It kinda takes all of the pressure off of me.”

Although Michelai, 33 had been in threesomes before, she was typically the person in the relationship inviting an additional body to the mix. But for the first time, she was going to be the third—and she was thrilled by the idea of it.

She was approached by a married couple on a trip to Vegas. "They were seeking me out, which also made me a little bit more confident and comfortable,” she says.

When it comes to threesomes, conversations usually revolve around experimenting sexually when you’re already in a relationship: What boundaries to discuss, whether it’s the right decision for your and your partner, and what aftercare may look like. It’s rare that the third person in the scenario is addressed. But communication, attention, and care are required for everyone involved, including the person joining just for the night.

“A ‘successful threesome’ isn’t about fulfilling the couple’s fantasy—unless that is explicitly discussed, negotiated, and consented to,” sex therapist Dr. Ty David Lerman, PhD tells Cosmopolitan. “Rather, it’s about all parties showing up as equals with all needs, desires, pleasure, and boundaries being honored.”

And when you do it right, it can be really hot and fun, without all of the responsibility that may come if you’re the one in the relationship.

“It kinda takes all of the pressure off of me,” Jess, 30 says.

Jess joined her best girlfriend and her situationship at the time. At first, it was just to watch them (which she really enjoyed). But eventually it turned into a regular hookup with the both of them.

Stepping into an established couple’s world could feel awkward, but Michelai says it didn’t. Because she’d been the “primary” woman before, she knew which questions to ask. “I made sure there were no unspoken rules,” she says. “I laid everything out on the table, and they laid everything out on the table.”

She also read the room. The husband was clearly letting his wife lead, so Michelai directed her questions to the wife before she ever approached him. And the husband’s etiquette in the moment won her over: “I really respected that he would straight-up ask her something in the middle of us doing something, like whether he could do this or that. I was like, ‘You know what? Hell yeah.’”

Jess, meanwhile, felt like a bit of an outsider at first—but only because she wanted to give her friend time to adjust. Since the threesome was her idea, she didn’t want to overstep. “The first time I was with them, I just watched,” she says. Afterward, her friend and the situationship asked her: Why didn’t you touch yourself? Why didn’t you join? “I didn’t want to overstep.”

Since then Jess has learned how important communication is to being a third.

“Communication is probably just as important as the threesome itself,” Michelai says. “You need to know what everyone wants, what everyone’s comfortable with, and what everyone is expecting the experience to be.”

She’s heard the horror stories of couples that only sought out a third to save the relationship or where boundaries were drawn around the man’s pleasure in an MFF.

“There’s a term in the polyamory community called ‘unicorn hunters,’” Dr. Lerman says. It’s reserved for a couple, usually heterosexual, seeking a third, usually a woman, to fulfill a fantasy, usually the man’s. In practice, he says, this often means the couple using the third for their own purposes. “The third feeling objectified, used by one or both of the couple, disempowered to really consent to the role they are playing for the couple, and often leaving unsatisfied.”

His fix is a stoplight system: green means hell yes, yellow means needs negotiation, red means hell no. He recommends running through it before anyone gets near a bedroom, and using it again mid-action, because consent is ongoing and can be revoked at any time. Or just ask, “How is everyone doing?” Simple, and it works.

But this doesn’t mean there’s a set routine that’s going to play out in the moment. “There’s this expectation that threesomes are all three people going at it equally, but I think it can be something a little bit more defined than that,” Jess says. She and her friend had decided beforehand that they wanted to “use him like a toy,”—something he had no issue with—so the two women didn’t hook up with each other. The rules can be unconventional as long as everyone agrees to them.

And as unsexy as it may seem to have a lot of discussion, it really pays off during the sex.

“We had conversations about everything before we got in the bedroom, so when we got in the bedroom, everything felt really organic,” Michelai says.

Being a third may seem more “relaxed” than being in the couple inviting another person in, but there are still instances where it might not be a fit.

A major red flag is if it’s obvious that the couple hasn’t talked to each other. “A major tell for the third in vetting a couple is if the couple has already had these conversations before you enter the picture,” Dr. Lerman says. “If they haven’t, don’t walk, run! It’s a glaring red flag that they do not know what they want, and they don’t have the communication skills to talk about it together, which means they sure aren’t going to be able to do that with you either.”

Things like double standards, rules that only apply to you, no conversation about sexual health, or any action that may make you feel like more of an accessory than a person.

“Pay attention to how the couple reacts when you say no, or voice a need, or your own boundary,” he says.

Michelai saw the flip side of this when she was the primary. She and her boyfriend brought in one of her best friends from college. “He was hyper-focused on her for like 10 minutes, and that was the longest 10 minutes of my life,” she says. She left the room. (“Should I have left? Probably not.”)

For the person who goes home alone, aftercare can be an afterthought, which is exactly the problem. Couples often assume that once the sexual interaction is over, it’s fine for the third to just get up and leave. But how would that feel in any other sexual scenario? Not so great, right?

Michelai explains that the married couple made sure to make her feel welcomed—without any awkward obligation to feel part of the relationship. “We definitely had the Kiki, cuddle, laughs, yap session after each time we had sex, and I felt very comfortable.” The wife even asked for alone time with her, so the two ordered champagne and took a bubble bath while the husband slept. “We didn’t have sex again without him, but we were cute, cuddly, making out, and had a really nice bubble bath.”

And when it was over, it was over. “I think we all happily had a great experience and happily went our separate ways,” she says.

Jess’s first time was a different story. The guy got weird afterward. “He was like, ‘OK, I’m just going to go to bed,’ and didn’t invite us to stay the night or ask how it went or anything like that, which was very jarring.” She and her friend salvaged the night with a debrief on the car ride home: How did you feel? Did you like that? It was hot when he did this. Ideally, she says, everyone would debrief together, or at least one-on-one.

Dr. Lerman says aftercare should be negotiated upfront, like everything else. “Good aftercare looks like starting that conversation ahead of any play,” he says. Will there be a puppy pile of cuddling? A text the next day? A second date to debrief? “If we can’t consent to aftercare, we don’t play. Simple.” Being the third adds a layer: what happens when the couple goes back to being a couple and you’re outside it? “Aftercare is ultimately about making sure nobody feels disposable once the clothes go back on.”

“I think you can suss out the vibe and feel the vibe between the couple to know if it’s a safe space to join in on,” Michelai says. She’s flattered when couples approach her, too. “That actually makes me feel more confident.”

Jess’s criteria are simple: both people have to be into it. “It wasn’t just one of the partners trying to do something sexually adventurous.” And she wants to be treated like a person. “These are real people that you’re probably going to be having a sexual encounter with, and they should be treated as such.” Couples can get a little fetishistic about a third, she says, but you can weed that out quickly by seeing whether both of them want to sit and talk with you like a real human.

“The most common mistake occurs when a couple takes on the mindset of ordering up a sexual experience rather than approaching this as a negotiation with all parties,” Dr. Lerman says says. Opening with a laundry list of rules the third has no say in creates a power imbalance from the jump. He also warns against expecting equal chemistry all around, which rarely happens. Be conscious of everyone and bring them all into the play, but let attraction go where it goes.

#6709. 22 Killer Watches I Saw at One of New York’s Most Exclusive Collector Hangs

This is an edition of the newsletter Box + Papers, Cam Wolf’s weekly deep dive into the world of watches. Sign up here.

I knew the watch collector meetup I was going to was legit when its organizer sent this text to the group: “We’ve engaged an off-duty NYPD detective to work security for our dinner. So, now really no reason not to bring your best!”

Last Wednesday night, at a fancy steakhouse in Midtown Manhattan, I was reminded why I love these enthusiast-organized events. This one was relatively small in comparison to blowouts like Rolliefest, but the idea was the same: A dozen or so collectors brought along their most prized timepieces and plunked them down on the table unattended (besides the off-duty NYPD detective, of course). When I asked one attendee if I could take his Breguet—similar to one heading to auction this weekend with a $73,000 estimate—across the room to take a photograph, he reacted like I’d asked if I could breathe oxygen: Of course! What a silly question. Events like these genuinely reflect the best of the hobby: deeply passionate collectors who really just want to share their watches with like-minded obsessives.

Between bites of miniature beef wellingtons and medium-rare steak, the guests passed around and ogled the dozens of grails on display. There were new classics on the table—including Vacheron Constantin’s Ultra-Thin, a leading contender for watch of the year—alongside plenty of old ones, including every flavor of vintage Rolex, from GMT-Masters to Daytonas to Explorer IIs. I was standing with one collector as he examined a pretty vintage Rolex GMT-Master. He stopped and looked around. So-and-so must be here, he muttered aloud. How did he know? Because he recognized the shade of the patina on the dial.

This particular group started getting together a couple of years ago, after the collectors @HorologicallyMinded, @s_h_lemon, @null_islands, and @jmsfisk (everyone at the event asked to remain anonymous) met at another watch-related retreat. @HorologicallyMinded, or HM, says that collecting was at one point something he did in solitude. “People generally judge when they learn how much watches cost,” HM tells me. “You paid how much for that!?” But he and the other three founders began meeting up for monthly dinners before eventually taking turns to organize these larger events. “This group has been the most rewarding part of this hobby,” HM says. “It’s been so great to have a group of people that have a common interest, but it’s not work-related and no one judges.”

Although the group has grown, the core four are still instrumental in making sure the functions go off without a hitch, with just the right spread of watches on the tables. “It is very deliberate and the four of us generally coordinate on it,” HM says. “We specifically make sure there is something for everyone.” That means ensuring there are at least a handful of watches worth less than $10,000—this time, that included several Rolex Datejusts, a Vulcain Cricket, and a gold Breitling from the 1940s. “We knew we were having some relative newbies and different people have different budgets, and we want everyone to be comfortable.” On the other end of the spectrum, some grail-level pieces were special requests from other members of the group.

All the watches wound up getting plenty of TLC. “I love the fact that we’re a group that can, and did, totally geek out about a vintage Longines Legend Diver, while a Doré dial Patek is on the same table,” HM says.

Below are some of the very best pieces I saw that night.

A Patek Philippe ref. 3970, part of the house’s historic lineage of pieces that combine a perpetual calendar with a chronograph. The dial on this one is so tasty.

A skeletonized Breguet Ref. 3355PT00PA0—maybe the watch of the night for me—on a show-stopping platinum bracelet.

A few years ago, MB&F started making more approachable versions of its sci-fi-ready watches and allocating them through a lottery system. This is the M.A.D2, with an outer ring on the dial that spins around very quickly. It’s really fun.

The aforementioned Rolex GMT-Master is a ref. 16760, a model produced during the ’80s that’s nicknamed the “Sophia Loren” thanks to its curvaceous profile.

Omega has incredible stuff in its archives. This is a chronograph from the ’30s that’s controlled entirely through that single button at 2 o’clock.

A couple of real bangers here. The Vacheron on the left is known as the “Cioccolatone,” because it resembles a square of chocolate. At the center is the Patek Philippe ref. 3417, an antimagnetic watch with just about the prettiest typography you’ll ever see on a watch. Zohran Mamdani should adopt that cursive for signs in the city, because it can make just about anything look nice: Warning: Rats. Or maybe, No Dumping Here.

A cloisonné dial from—of all brands—IWC! I am such a sucker for a cloisonné, which refers to the intricate images carefully fashioned from wire and colorful baked enamel.

A beautiful example of one of the Seafarers that Heuer made for Abercrombie & Fitch from the ’50s through the ’70s, back when the latter was still a rugged outdoor outfitter. The shades of orange, yellow, and blue are dreamy.

A monochromatic take on the Audemars Piguet Royal Oak Perpetual Calendar, which was produced in the ’80s and ’90s but looks incredibly modern.

Universal Genève finally relaunched last year after decades on the shelf, but it’s hard to beat the originals. This Polerouter comes on an extremely cool “wave” bracelet, which basically uses a repeating chevron pattern to make the slinky bit of metal appear to be in motion.

During World War II, a dozen watch manufacturers came together to make models following a strict set of specifications for the British Ministry of Defence. One of those brands was Longines, which produced this strapping piece.

You didn’t think we’d wrap this list up without a gorgeous yellow-gold Daytona, did you?

The ultimate fusion of sport and luxury watches. Heuer supplied this ’70s-era Carrera to Ferrari’s racing team, including legendary drivers like Jacky Ickx, Niki Lauda, and Clay Regazzoni.

This Patek is cool, but the bracelet is insane.

This isn’t your average Patek Philippe Nautilus. PP began producing this reference 3800 in 1981 as a smaller counterpart to the original. The few times I’ve gotten to try one on, I’m always struck by how perfect the proportions are. It’s nice and thin and looks just right on the wrist.

The United States Merchant Marines’ logo really punches up this Day-Date.

The ref. 6541 is the most beloved version of the Rolex Milgauss. It was produced in the ’50s and features a signature honeycomb dial. One sold for $2.5 million at auction in 2023.

Is there a better way to time your yacht race than with this Heuer Skipper? Probably not.

It’s good to have doubles, especially when it comes to vintage Rolex Explorer IIs.

#6707. Going Home—A Day in the Life With Libby Taverner As She Walks the Chanel Show in Sydney

One of Australia’s buzziest models, Libby Taverner made her runway debut during the fall 2025 season. Since then, her career has been a frenetic blur. For spring 2027, she walked no fewer than 27 shows, Matthieu Blazy’s Chanel among them. When the storied French house decided to reprise its resort 2027 show in Sydney, it was no surprise the 20-year-old was given a ring.

The Sydney show not only marked a significant moment for Chanel—it was their first Australian outing since 1982—but also for the young model. “It’s still relatively early in my journey of living overseas. Being able to come home and walk a Chanel show in Australia feels incredibly special, and it’s an opportunity that I honestly didn’t imagine would come around so soon,” she told Vogue.

“There’s just a little sparkle in my heart knowing that I’m doing something so incredible in my home country. It makes me feel really proud,” she added.

For Taverner, the show meant that she could serve as a guide to her fellow model friends and industry peers, many of whom were experiencing their first times Down Under. Lucky for them, Taverner considers herself an expert at all things Australia, as she grew up in multiple parts of the country. “I was born in Gladstone, Queensland, before my family decided to travel around Australia,” she says. “We spent a couple of years in Perth and Bundaberg too.”

Her top Sydney recommendation? Hitting the Australian coastline. “There’s something for everyone, whether you want to swim, surf, or go for a coastal walk, or simply spend some time relaxing in the sun.” Catching the sunset at the beach with some fish and chips or and a pitstop at Yo-Chi for some fro-yo are must-dos too. “It’s such a simple thing, but to me it’s a very quintessential Australian experience.”

But most importantly for those wanting the full Aussie experience, Taverner recommends taking a step back and slowing down. “The best way to experience Australia is to slow down, explore a little, and embrace that relaxed outdoor lifestyle that we’re so lucky to have.”

Below, a day in the life of Libby Taverner as she gets ready to walk the Chanel resort 2027 reprise show in Sydney.

Fashion week is always such an exciting whirlwind, with everyone traveling from different parts of the world and moving from one city to the next. But there’s something different about walking in Sydney. It feels a little more personal, and I think there’s an added sense of gratitude because I get to experience this moment somewhere that means so much to me. It’s a feeling I don't think I’ll forget anytime soon.

Reading Ugly Love by Colleen Hoover while getting my hair done for the show.

Doing a walkthrough for the rehearsals in the show space.

The scenic walk to the venue from the hotel. If the weather is nice, I'd love to squeeze in another beach visit and a swim. I think that's one of the things I miss most when I'm living in Europe, so any opportunity to get back into the ocean is always a good one!

Doing my morning skincare routine to make myself look awake and fresh for the show.

Sun break while waiting in between shows.

My fabulous look. For the show, I was wearing a black bodysuit layered with a beautiful black coat/dress. It’s a very timeless, classy and chic look, which I absolutely love. There’s something about an all-black outfit that feels so effortlessly elegant.

Accessories pic, showing my favorite part of my outfit. It has such a fun texture and color that really stands out. I love that little contrast and it’s one of those details that adds a bit of personality and makes the whole look feel so special.

My number in the lineup for show and my show shoes.

Finished the show and ready for the afterparty!

#6706. Stylist Soki Mak on 10 Things That Inspired Kim Kardashian’s All’s Fair Season Two Wardrobe

From 1990s Helmut Newton shoots to classic Bond girls to unexpected Comme des Garçons finds

In fashion, anything from niche archival research to a favorite film to an outfit you saw on your morning commute can make for inspiration. In our new series 10 Things, we ask industry professionals and tastemakers to divulge the (you guessed it) 10 things that had the most impact on their aesthetic choices.

The second season of Ryan Murphy’s legal drama, All’s Fair, opened with reality star-turned-actor Kim Kardashian in a patchwork Alexander McQueen suit. The rare ensemble, composed of a peplum jacket and fluted skirt, came from Lee McQueen’s theatrical Spring 2004 collection, titled Deliverance, in which models danced down the runway in shimmering gowns, dramatic feathered skirts, and tulle galore. “There were comments about Kim’s clothing being inappropriate in the workplace, but that’s what it should be,” Soki Mak, the visionary behind Kardashian’s Allura Grant character, told Harper’s Bazaar. “If I’m going to watch a show, I want to be like, ‘What the hell is that?’”

When Mak first joined the All’s Fair team—handpicked by Kardashian, via Instagram, to dress her onscreen as a high-powered lawyer—she had never ventured into costume design. The stylist, who has worked with everyone from Rosalía to Pamela Anderson, spent the first season developing the visual identity of Allura, merging her client’s own flair for shock value and fantasy with the limited character descriptions she received. We saw hyper-cinched waists and archival Jean Paul Gaultier; Hermès Birkins and suits with exposed thongs. It was Kardashian, with a twist.

But for Season Two, Mak focused on separating Kardashian from her character, tracking Allura’s emotional journey through darker color palettes and less expected silhouettes. She dug deeper into designer archives, emerging with moody gems from some of the most beloved collections of the ’90s and early-aughts. Rare vintage pieces from Maison Margiela, Comme des Garçons, Yohji Yamamoto, and Alaïa each made their cameos.

Ahead, the stylist dives into 10 influences that shaped Allura’s costume design, from Kim Kardashian herself to classic Bond girls to a baker-boy cap she had to fight for.

[For Season One,] no one gave us any sort of visual references. I’d never been a costume designer before, but usually, when I’ve worked on character-based stuff—I used to work a lot with Nadia Lee Cohen—we would develop the character first, so when I go into styling, it’s quite easy to visualize that person. There was no time for that, and there was no visual reference for Allura. So, when I came in, I was just thinking, “Okay, what do I see her as?” I looked at Kim personally, and she’s this fantasy. There is no one like her. So I’m like, “Okay, if you have all of the money in the world and all of the access in the world, all the power in the world, what would you look like?”

I’ve always thought of Kim as someone that creates and shocks and is the first to do something, whether people like it or not. And that’s the energy I wanted to go into this with. She challenges the norm. I’ve also always been a big believer in trying to be a trendsetter rather than a follower. In some of these moments, I would find it difficult to make a mood board because the references weren’t there. That was where I would say to Kim, “Trust me.”

For Season One, we started reaching out to brands, and Jean Paul Gaultier was [the first to say], “Let’s do it.” The minute we had them, the whole narrative of the show changed. They went deep into the archives and started sending these looks that hadn’t been worn in 20 years. It was amazing. We were sourcing vintage and archival pieces on the side, but we really focused on Jean Paul Gaultier because everything else compared to that just looked sad.

When the images started circulating from the first season, a critic that I respect wrote that the fashion was “kind of obvious.” Although I disagreed, I understood where he was coming from. Maybe Kim wearing a Mugler suit that accentuated her body and her curves was something we had seen her wear before. This season, I wanted to do something really different. I wanted to go less out-there with the colors and a little less predictable with the shapes and the styling. I picked designers and pieces that weren’t obvious choices, and I think it showed growth from last season. We took it somewhere else completely.

For hair and makeup references, I would go on Pinterest and pull old Helmut Newton shoots because I wanted it to look very timeless. I think that was the key. Everything looked … not minimal, there was definitely no minimal… but very ’90s-based and gorgeous.

Kim loves Madonna. There were a lot of old Madonna images for her platinum hair and makeup, a lot of which was done by Pat McGrath.

I think I’d made a point this year that I wanted to take it down a dark route. I almost wanted Allura to be like, “I just had a shit experience in the first season My man’s left me. I’m pissed off. I’ve gone away, and I’ve come back, and I’m serious now.” So everything’s much more covered up. There are darker layers. She’s experimenting. When I was going through the [recent] runway shows, everything was very pink and quite eclectic, so we mainly went with archival pieces. I used a lot of really rare Yohji Yamamoto, Comme des Garçons, and Lee McQueen.

There was a Margiela skirt suit [from the Spring 1994 collection, Retrospective] and it was just very kitsch. It was a long skirt with a suit jacket and was paired with a black leather baker boy hat from Hermès. We were in a bidding war with a collector in Japan. When we were filming the scene, someone in production or maybe Ryan [Murphy] had mentioned they wanted to tone down the hats for this season. But I got that memo after styling the look, and I was adamant that the look needed the hat. I begged. And then she sat at the table wearing a hat and I could see everyone was like, “How is she getting to wear a hat?” I just felt like the look needed it. It took [Kardashian] out of her normal visual stance and how she usually portrays herself.

Comme des Garçons is very destructive and not really tailored to fit a woman’s body in the way [Kardashian] usually likes. And we got her in [a gray jacket and long lilac-gray column skirt] and worked it around her body. She never once made any comments. She would just look at herself for a second and be like, “Cool.” And then go on set.

I have to let Kris Jenner take credit for [Elizabeth Taylor’s 1969 Scorpio cape, worn by Kardashian in Episode 1], because that’s her cape. She would come to set all the time and once had a conversation with Ryan about the fact that she has this cape. He was like, “That’s it, we need it.” From there, we shipped in a $10 million diamond that was most similar to what Elizabeth Taylor was wearing [in original imagery]. It was flown into L.A. in someone’s pocket, and we had it on set for like five days with Kim’s security. It’s a piece of history. It’s really special. Each day, it would go to Kim and then back in her car home because no one wanted to take responsibility for it.

In general, a lot of my choices in clothing and costume referenced old Bond films where the women were super sexual and curvy and had Brigitte Bardot hair. There was glamour, sex, opulence, money. The outfits were completely inappropriate and not really wearable in everyday life. But if I’m going to watch a show, that’s what I want to see. I want to be like, “What the hell? What is that?” There were comments about Kim’s clothing being inappropriate in the workplace, but that’s what it should be. It’s fun.

#6705. The 6 Best Hair Rollers for Supermodel Volume

Salon-level bounce, no appointment necessary.

We may earn commission from links on this page, but we only recommend products we love. Promise.

If you've ever been envious of a big, bouncy blowout à la a ’90s supermodel, I have amazing news: Those angelic waves are actually pretty simple to recreate—no salon visit required, promise! Even if you don't have the skills of a professional celebrity stylist (because I definitely don't), you can still achieve tons of volume with the right hair routine and the best hair rollers.

If you’re after va-va-volume, using your thermal round brush, multi-styler, or blow dryer on its own simply won’t cut it. A set of hair rollers is the key to long-lasting volume. As a long-haired beauty editor who loves nothing more than the way my hair looks after a salon blowout, I've tried pretty much every type of hair roller out there to DIY those same coveted waves at home. I also tapped expert hairstylists to share how to properly use these root-lifting tools, below.

Why we love it: These ceramic Velcro rollers are perfect for achieving that bouncy blowout look. They come in three different sizes so you can easily place them around the head, with the smallest being perfect for shorter layers and bangs. You won't have to worry about them falling out of your hair, either, since they're made with a self-grip surface and don't require any clips. Just roll ’em up, and you’re good to go.

Why we love it: Want to keep your hair effortlessly voluminous on the go? (Who doesn’t?!) Mane’s travel-friendly roller set will ensure your mane (heh) stays bouncy, no matter where you are in the world. The barrels on this six-piece set are self-gripping, too, so there’s no need to pack extra clips that are bound to get lost in the bottom of a bag.

Why we love it: If you've got a lot of hair, first, consider yourself blessed, but you might need more than the standard six-to-nine set of rollers. Luckily, this convenient kit comes with 36 (!!!) along with 18 metal clips to lock them in place. There are also long- and short-hair size options, so if you've got a bob, creating the perfect curls and waves will still be a breeze.

Beauty editor Beth Gillette loves the smallest size for her super-fine bixie lengths, “These are so gentle on my hair, even as I pull them out—I can see why the Pheloung sisters have such good hair,” she explains. “But I especially love the range of sizes and how many come in this chic case.”

Why we love it: If you want XXL volume without needing to re-wet your hair, a set of heated rollers is a one-and-done way to get the look of a defined blowout on already-dry hair. Not only do the T3 hot rollers have a dual temperature setting, but they have cool-grip edges, so you won't burn your precious fingers while setting them in place. The set even comes in a sleek case and has an auto-off setting—no need to question if you left them on while you're out at dinner (we’ve all been there).

Why we love it: While most rollers are made of plastic, these are constructed out of metal, which evenly distributes heat and really locks in the volume when you’re blowing out your hair at home. You might think that metal would slip right off your mane, but these have a self-grip exterior that latches onto your hair. (The set does come with clips if you need some extra support, though.) You shouldn’t be surprised if your hair still looks voluminous two or three days after using these.

Why we love it: Sure, you can sleep in hair rollers, but you probably won’t get a good night’s sleep. (I’m speaking from experience.) If you're looking for a comfortable method that will ensure tons of volume and gorgeous waves, look no further than Kitsch's Heatless Curling Set. It's made of soft satin, so there's no pulling or tugging, and it comes with two matching scrunchies to hold your hair perfectly in place overnight. When someone compliments your hair, you can literally say "I woke up like this."

Every hair roller is different, and each hair type will require unique steps. However, it's a good idea to keep these expert-recommended tips in mind if you're looking to achieve a bouncy blowout at home:

"The way your curlers and hair sets is the way that it is going to flow," explains Tippi Shorter, celebrity hairstylist and Mizani global artistic director. "Place the rollers at the crown of the head and roll your hair under the curler; that way, you will get more volume and body."

Joseph Maine, celebrity stylist and artistic director of Color Wow Hair, suggests using a brush and rollers that are on the larger side in order to achieve a smoother bouncy blowout. "The smaller they are, the more curls they're going to leave in your hair."

Use a diffuser attachment on a blow dryer to gently heat the rollers back up after each one has been placed. This will ensure that they are set perfectly. Then, keep the rollers in your hair for about 15 minutes or until they cool down completely.

In short: There’s no one-size-fits-all roller, and each type serves a slightly different purpose. You probably have seen quite a few throwback pics of supermodels getting glammed up with Velcro rollers, but times have changed, and rollers have evolved.

Hot and heatless rollers can be used to create the effortless and bouncy look you're going for—it just depends on the size of the roller and the process you use. And remember, the bigger the roller, the bouncier the hair. That means the smaller the roller, the tighter the curls will be.

Additionally, some rollers are made from ceramic or metal, while others are made of plastic. The ceramic and metal distribute heat better and are able to boost and lock in volume more easily. The plastic rollers are also effective, but their effects don’t last as long.

It depends on the type of roller you use and what your desired final look is. For example, if you’re hoping to create heatless curls, stick with satin or plastic rollers and sleep with them overnight for defined ringlets come morning. All rollers can boost volume, and if you want to restore bounce, they should be used on dry hair to lift your roots.

"Most people need to have extra moisture in the hair in order to get a hair roller style to stay," says Maine. To ensure that your hair is properly hydrated, apply blowout mousse, spray, or leave-in conditioner before styling.

#6703. Martine Rose Is Balenciaga’s New Creative Director

Martine Rose is Balenciaga's new creative director. The London-based designer will start on November 16, taking over the French-Spanish label from Pierpaolo Piccioli, whose departure was announced yesterday after three seasons at the house.

It's the first time Martine Rose has taken charge of a major fashion house, but it isn't her first Balenciaga gig. She worked as a menswear consultant under Demna from 2015 to 2018, helping shape the oversized proportions and left-field clothes that defined his early years at the brand. Now she's returning with control of the whole enterprise.

“It is a true privilege to be appointed creative director of Balenciaga, a house with an extraordinary heritage and a fearless creative spirit,” Rose said in a statement. “Balenciaga has been shaped by remarkable creative talents before me. I am committed to honoring this legacy and look forward to creating the next chapter in this rich and beautiful story.”

Rose founded her eponymous label in 2007 and has built it into one of the most influential brands in British fashion. Her collections pull from soccer and nightlife club culture, music, and the everyday wardrobes of London dwellers: suits get stretched out or squeezed in, tracksuits become tailoring, loafers turn into mules. It's menswear, on her terms.

Through her career, Rose has collaborated with Nike, Clarks, Supreme, Stüssy, and Tommy Hilfiger, and her clothes have been worn by everyone from Kendrick Lamar to Lewis Hamilton to Timothée Chalamet. But despite her idiosyncratic influence over what menswear looks like now, Rose has yet to have worked the top job at a house of Balenciaga's size. Her appointment makes her the first woman to lead the brand in its 109-year history. Her appointment makes her the first woman to lead the brand in its 109-year history.

“Martine Rose embodies this spirit with a fresh, fearless and deeply contemporary vision,” said Kering CEO Luca de Meo. “Her connection to the new generation and her instinctive understanding of culture bring a new dimension to the house.”

It's a big appointment, and one fashion people have wanted for a long time. Rumors that Rose had signed with Balenciaga have been swirling for weeks, but now it's official. The house hasn't yet said when her first collection will arrive, but whenever it does, we'll all be watching.
